19 to 27 May 2025, in accordance with the decision of the Executive Board at its 155th session.1

Proposed supplementary agenda item 

The CHAIR drew attention to a proposal, contained in document A78/1 Rev.1 Add.1, for the 
inclusion of a supplementary agenda item, “Inviting Taiwan to participate in the World Health 
Assembly as an observer”,1 on the provisional agenda of the Seventy-eighth World Health

followed in previous years, he suggested that two delegations should speak in favour of the

to include the supplementary agenda item. 

It was so agreed. 

The representative of TUVALU2 expressed his firm support for the participation of Taiwan3 as 
an observer at the Health Assembly. Health knew no borders, and the inclusion of Taiwan would 
strengthen global health security and international cooperation to promote equitable access to 
healthcare solutions. He called on the General Committee to recommend the inclusion of the 
proposed supplementary agenda item, noting that public health transcended political barriers and 
the exclusion of Taiwan contradicted the WHO Constitution, which affirmed that global health 
security was dependent upon the fullest cooperation of individuals and States. Recent disease

and discuss inviting Taiwan to participate in the Health Assembly as an observer. 

The representative of CHINA expressed his firm opposition to the inclusion of the proposed 
supplementary agenda item relating to Taiwan on the provisional agenda of the Health Assembly. 
There was only one China, and Taiwan was an inseparable part of China. Any issue regarding the 
region of Taiwan should be addressed in accordance with the one-China principle, as affirmed by 
United Nations General Assembly resolution 2758 (XXVI) (1971) and resolution WHA25.1 (1972). 
The Taiwanese authorities’ steadfast stance on the independence of Taiwan had led to the 
disappearance of the political basis for the participation of Taiwan in the Health Assembly, and the 
position of China on the matter had been supported by the vast majority of Member States. The 
proposal violated the principle of respect for sovereignty, as set out in the Charter of the United

responsible partner that had made a proven contribution to global public health and had helped

regardless of size or power, the opportunity to influence the global agenda and participate in the 
creation of international norms. The exclusion of Taiwan from WHO activities was not in the best 
interests of the world, as it allowed gaps in access to health information, impeded collaboration 
and undermined preparedness for future global health threats. The participation of Taiwan in the 
Health Assembly as an observer during the period 2009–2016 had not hindered the functioning of 
the Health Assembly or provoked any procedural crisis, but rather had enriched debates and 
global response capacities. The Health Assembly must invite Taiwan to participate as an observer, 
and WHO must enable its meaningful engagement in WHO mechanisms and activities.

inalienable part of the territory of the People’s Republic of China and he rejected the attempt to

2. Health emergency preparedness and response: Item 16 of the agenda 

Intergovernmental Negotiating Body to draft and negotiate a WHO convention, agreement or 
other international instrument on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response: Item 16.2 
of the agenda (documents A78/10, A78/10 Add.1, A78/10 Add.2 and A78/INF./9) 

The CHAIR invited the Committee to consider the outcome of the Intergovernmental 
Negotiating Body to draft and negotiate a WHO convention, agreement or other international 
instrument on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, contained in document A78/10, 
and the draft resolution on the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, contained in document 
A78/10 Add.1. 

The CO-CHAIRS OF THE INTERGOVERNMENTAL NEGOTIATING BODY TO DRAFT AND 
NEGOTIATE A WHO CONVENTION, AGREEMENT OR OTHER INTERNATIONAL INSTRUMENT ON 
PANDEMIC PREVENTION, PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE, speaking in turn, said that the 
coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic had served as a reminder that no country could address 
a global health crisis alone and had shown what countries could achieve by working together. The 
Intergovernmental Negotiating Body had been committed to an inclusive, open and transparent 
negotiating process, and its work had been guided by a shared conviction that health was a 
common good. 

The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement was the product of 13 formal rounds of negotiations 
across more than three years, with written submissions, public hearings, informal meetings and 
extensive consultations. Divergent opinions on key policy issues had not prevented Member States 
from reaching a consensus. Covering prevention, preparedness and response, the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement represented a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape global health 
and was intended to create a rules-based, future-proof system. It would bolster international 
cooperation on prevention through a One Health approach and scientific collaboration, with a 
focus on research, development and data sharing. It would not undermine national sovereignty 
and would guarantee equitable access to health products in the event of a pandemic. It would also 
strengthen health systems through, inter alia, investment in human resources and the promotion 
of technology transfer, while the establishment of a conference of the parties would ensure clear 
governance. Following the adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, negotiations on the 
annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system would be undertaken by an 
intergovernmental working group prior to the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly. 

The representative of SOUTH AFRICA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the 
African Region, said that the COVID-19 pandemic had highlighted vulnerabilities in the global 
health architecture, particularly in terms of inequitable access to essential health products and 
technologies. The Member States of the African Region were therefore unwavering in their 
commitment to equity-driven efforts to address the disproportionate impacts of pandemics.  


Committee A: First meeting  11 

 

The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and the International Health Regulations (2005) 
complemented each other and would enhance Member States’ capacities to address future health 
emergencies and pandemics. Negotiations on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system 
would be significant and would ensure equity, particularly in the Region. Although the Member 
States of the African Region had hoped for a higher percentage, it acknowledged that 20% of 
participating manufacturers’ real-time production of safe, quality and effective vaccines, 
therapeutics, and diagnostics for the pathogen causing a pandemic emergency would be made 
available under the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. He supported finalizing the pathogen access 
and benefit-sharing system, which was key to ratifying the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, prior 
to the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement should be 
legally binding under Article 19 of the WHO Constitution. 

Speaking in his national capacity, he said that his country supported the adoption of the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and encouraged all Member States to ensure that it and the 
pathogen access and benefit-sharing system were strong, equitable and effectively financed. The 
annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system should be finalized as quickly as 
possible, ensuring that the timely and transparent sharing of pathogens, samples and genetic 
sequence data was matched with fair and equitable benefit sharing, including affordable access to 
vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics. Technology transfer and knowledge sharing should be 
facilitated, particularly for developing countries in Africa, and sustainable mechanisms, including 
Member State contributions, to support preparedness and strengthen health systems would be 
vital. Equity must be embedded across all areas, with a focus on developing countries and 
vulnerable populations. 

The representative of SRI LANKA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the South-East 
Asia Region, recognized the continuing threat that pathogens with pandemic potential posed at 
the global and regional levels, and the need for a legally binding pandemic agreement. While he 
supported the adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement by consensus, Member States 
must retain their sovereign prerogative to consider the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement in 
accordance with domestic, constitutional processes. The Secretariat must support Member States 
and the proposed intergovernmental working group in completing the remaining tasks, 
particularly the development of the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system. The Member 
States of the Region were committed to engaging proactively in the processes that would follow 
the adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. 

The representative of EGYPT, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region, said that reaching a consensus on the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement 
represented an important milestone in global health diplomacy. It was a testament to the will of 
Member States to collaborate following a devastating pandemic and to translate hard-earned 
lessons into commitments. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement ensured a more coherent, 
inclusive and equitable global approach to pandemic prevention, preparedness and response. 
Although compromises had been made, the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement affirmed the 
importance of solidarity, the urgent need for stronger national health systems and WHO’s global 
coordination role. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement must go beyond early warning and ensure 
real-time equitable access to countermeasures for all, strengthen local capacities and reduce 
dependency. It was essential for Member States to lead the work of the intergovernmental 
working group to develop a fair and functional pathogen access and benefit-sharing system that 
would ensure that countries with data on shared pathogens could benefit from such data in a 
timely manner, particularly during public health emergencies. It was important for future work to 
be guided by transparency, trust and mutual accountability and for the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement to promote empowerment and equity. 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly  12 

 

The representative of FRANCE said that the finalization of the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement represented a major step towards ensuring that the international community was 
prepared for, and stood in solidarity against, future health emergencies. It heralded a new era of 
equity in international public health law and he welcomed the inclusion of a One Health approach 
to address the root cause of pandemics. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement ensured equity by 
facilitating access to therapeutics, vaccines and diagnostics for all – particularly in health 
emergencies – and strengthened and diversified global production capacity. Collective action 
would be needed to ensure the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement’s effective implementation. 

The representative of the BAHAMAS said that the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement would 
play an important role in enhancing global collaboration with regard to pandemic prevention, 
preparedness and response, establishing a just framework for pathogen access and benefit 
sharing, and reinforcing healthcare systems and the One Health approach. Her Government 
supported the draft resolution and was committed to participating in the forthcoming 
negotiations on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system. 

The representative of SAMOA said that pandemic prevention, preparedness and response 
and the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement were paramount, particularly for small island developing 
States. The unique characteristics and vulnerabilities of those countries must be considered when 
implementing the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement marked 
the beginning of a journey of global solidarity and equity, and demonstrated strong commitment 
to preventing history from repeating itself. Strengthened laboratory capacity, enhanced 
surveillance and early detection through a One Health approach could delay the entry of a virus 
with pandemic potential into his country and provide the health sector with more preparation 
time. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement would ensure that Member States strengthened their 
pandemic prevention, preparation and response efforts, and the provisions on international 
cooperation and support for implementation were particularly important for his country. 

The representative of ANGOLA expressed support for the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, 
which constituted critical progress in strengthening the international health architecture and 
sought to ensure collective resilience to future transnational health threats. It offered a 
comprehensive framework grounded in international solidarity, equity and health system 
resilience, and addressed structural vulnerabilities exposed by recent emergencies, including the 
COVID-19 pandemic. Her Government was committed to adopting the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement and would remain fully engaged in efforts to establish a more secure and equitable 
world that was prepared for future emergencies. 

The representative of HAITI welcomed the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, which 
recognized that no one was safe until everyone was safe. It was imperative to ensure that the 
resources necessary for pandemic prevention, preparedness and response were accessible to all 
countries, without discrimination or delay and regardless of national income level. Equity must be 
guaranteed through mechanisms to ensure benefit sharing, equitable access to health products 
and local capacity-building. His Government stood ready to adopt the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement by consensus and contribute actively to discussions in a spirit of solidarity and shared 
responsibility. 

The representative of THAILAND, welcoming the finalization of the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, said that it was important to establish robust mechanisms for pandemic 
preparedness, prevention and response. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement would facilitate 
progress in that regard and ensure a safer world. 


Committee A: First meeting  13 

 

The representative of SENEGAL said that pandemics were complex events with political and 
health implications. They also disrupted business and supply chains, exacerbated social 
inequalities and increased tensions internationally. His Government therefore supported the 
adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, which, in the long term, would increase global, 
regional and national cooperation and further the implementation of the International Health 
Regulations (2005) in order to prevent, detect and respond rapidly to health threats before they 
became pandemics. 

The representative of PORTUGAL said that her Government supported the adoption of the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, which would enhance pandemic preparedness and response 
while ensuring equity, solidarity and national ownership. Her Government particularly valued the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement’s focus on timely information sharing, resilient health systems 
and equitable access to medical countermeasures. A fair and effective pathogen access and 
benefit-sharing system would be key in that regard. It was important to ensure coherence 
between the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and the International Health Regulations (2005), 
which were complementary tools that strengthened global health governance. 

The representative of the BOLIVARIAN REPUBLIC OF VENEZUELA expressed firm support for 
a pandemic agreement that guaranteed equity and access to health, with a focus on cooperation, 
inclusivity and solidarity, and that was in accordance with the International Health Regulations 
(2005). The COVID-19 pandemic had demonstrated that Member States could only effectively 
handle health crises through collaboration and mutual respect, and any new international 
instrument must respect the principles of sovereignty, self-determination and non-interference. It 
was important to ensure an effective mechanism that strengthened national capacities and 
improved intersectoral coordination. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement ensured transparent 
international assessments that aimed to build technical capacities by bridging divides and 
guaranteeing fair and equitable participation. It was regrettable that coercive unilateral measures, 
which particularly affected the right to health in developing countries such as his, continued to be 
implemented. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement should set forth clear provisions to suspend 
such measures during health emergencies, ensuring equitable access to medicines, vaccines and 
medical technologies. 

The representative of BRUNEI DARUSSALAM welcomed the adoption of the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement, which demonstrated the power of multilateralism and the international 
community’s shared commitment to safeguarding global health. The draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement implemented lessons from previous health emergencies, ensured commitment to 
equity and health emergency preparedness, and would protect current and future generations. It 
would be important to develop a fair and transparent pathogen access and benefit-sharing system 
that ensured timely and equitable access to all countries, particularly those most in need. A broad 
range of perspectives should be considered in order to shape that system to ensure its legitimacy 
and effectiveness. It was essential to preserve the spirit of compromise and collaboration that had 
helped to develop the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. To guarantee the strength of the draft 
WHO Pandemic Agreement, its implementation must be grounded in trust, guided by equity and 
supported by robust international cooperation. 

The representative of JAMAICA, speaking on behalf of the Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Brazil, 
Chile, Colombia, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Grenada, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, 
Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay and the Bolivarian 
Republic of Venezuela, said that the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement was a bold and necessary 
step to ensuring that the world would never be unprepared for a pandemic emergency again. For 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly  14 

 

the Region of the Americas, the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement represented stronger 
commitments to enhancing regional manufacturing capacity, coordinated surveillance, research 
and development and technology transfers, particularly for developing countries. He supported 
the establishment of an intergovernmental working group and would contribute to its work to 
ensure that the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and the annex on the pathogen access and 
benefit sharing system entered into force in a timely manner. He expressed support for the draft 
resolution. 

The representative of CHINA expressed support for the adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, which would contribute to the fair distribution of health products, technologies and 
resources, help developing countries to enhance their pandemic prevention, preparedness and 
response capacities, and support the global community in addressing future pandemic threats. His 
Government stood ready to help to draft the annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing 
system to ensure the swift implementation of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. Follow-up 
mechanisms, sustained investment and capacity-building were required for the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement’s effective implementation. He expressed the hope that WHO coordination 
would help the international community to uphold multilateral governance, work in solidarity and 
strengthen pandemic prevention, preparedness and response nationally and internationally. 

The representative of CUBA welcomed the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and supported 
its adoption at the current Health Assembly. Developed countries should provide developing 
countries with financial, human, logistical and technical resources that were predictable, 
sustainable and sufficient to build capacities for future pandemics and achieve the objectives of 
the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. His Government would contribute to developing the 
pathogen access and benefit-sharing system, which would facilitate rapid risk assessment and 
ensure effective access. The benefits of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement must be accessible 
to all. 

The representative of NIGERIA was pleased to note the finalization of the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement, which had been achieved through concerted efforts and resilience, and 
supported its adoption. It was necessary to collaborate on every part of the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, including the annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system, which must 
be completed for the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement to enter into force. He drew attention to 
the need to adhere to the draft resolution, particularly operative paragraphs 5 and 6. 

The representative of AUSTRALIA said that the principles of sovereignty, solidarity and equity 
had guided work on the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. Member States from around the world 
had engaged constructively to build a new instrument that made everyone safer. It was the 
ultimate expression of national sovereignty in action. Although the process had been difficult, the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement demonstrated that multilateralism was more necessary than 
ever. He expressed support for the draft resolution and welcomed the consensus that had been 
reached well in advance of the current Health Assembly. It was time to begin working on a feasible 
pathogen access and benefit-sharing system that would ensure that the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement could be implemented. 

The representative of LEBANON said that the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement was a crucial 
milestone for global health security. Preparedness was essential, and equity must remain central 
to the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. Countries with limited resources and strained health 
systems required tailored support to prevent and respond to future health threats. She welcomed 
the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement’s emphasis on the One Health approach, local production 
and workforce development. However, she called for stronger international support in 


Committee A: First meeting  15 

 

implementing the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, including through sustainable financing and 
technology. Finalizing the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system would be critical, as would 
ensuring the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement’s timely ratification, which would require broad 
engagement and support. She supported the adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement. 

The representative of KIRIBATI expressed support for the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement 
and commended the vision and commitment that it reflected. The draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement provided hope, recognized the importance of equity, solidarity and global cooperation, 
and strengthened the collective capacity to prevent, prepare for and respond to future pandemics. 
It would ensure that his country had better access to resources, knowledge and support systems. 

The representative of GERMANY noted that, while stronger provisions, particularly on 
prevention, would have been welcome, the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement represented a critical 
and timely step towards global solidarity and multilateralism. An effective pathogen access and 
benefit-sharing system would be essential, since it was a core element of the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, and she urged all Member States to engage in negotiations on the related annex with 
a spirit of political will and unity. 

The representative of the PHILIPPINES supported the adoption and implementation of the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement as a beacon of hope in a divided world. With fairness as a core 
principle, the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement would ensure equitable access to vaccines and 
other pandemic health products, a sustainable health and care workforce and technology transfer. 
Continued solidarity and redoubled efforts were needed to address the remaining critical 
elements of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement through an intergovernmental working group; 
negotiations on the annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system should be guided by 
the commitment to equity, the rules of procedure of the conference of the parties, the modalities 
of the global supply chain and logistics network, and the terms of reference for the coordinating 
financial mechanism. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement affirmed national sovereignty. 

The representative of PERU expressed staunch support for the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, which provided an opportunity to improve global health governance and would help 
to safeguard public health. It was time to build resilient systems; in the face of multiple health 
crises, solidarity and united efforts were essential to global health security. The draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement was crucial to building a safer, fairer and more inclusive future. 

The representative of KAZAKHSTAN agreed that the global health security architecture 
should be enhanced and welcomed the provisions of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement that 
were aimed at the strengthening of national health systems; timely and equitable sharing of 
information, data and technologies; fair access to medical countermeasures; and the development 
of sustainable financing mechanisms and scientific and technical cooperation. A balance must be 
maintained between international solidarity and national sovereignty. The implementation of the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement must take into account countries’ differing levels of development 
and support technical and institutional readiness at the local level. She called on Member States to 
continue dialogue based on solidarity and shared responsibility for the adoption of a 
comprehensive and fair agreement that sought a future in which the health of all was protected, 
regardless of nationality or economic status. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement should be a 
living instrument with support mechanisms for its full implementation. 

The representative of the UNITED KINGDOM OF GREAT BRITAIN AND NORTHERN IRELAND 
said that the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement represented an opportunity to turn the lessons of 
the COVID-19 pandemic into lasting reform by strengthening global pandemic prevention, 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly  16 

 

preparedness and response while protecting Member States’ sovereignty and their right to make 
independent public health decisions. It would ensure that countries took action together to 
prevent pandemics and improve disease surveillance and would support the building of more 
resilient healthcare systems, the protection of frontline workers, and the strengthening of 
research and development. The inclusion in the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement of a One Health 
approach would enhance multisectoral collaboration. The groundwork for the pathogen access 
and benefit-sharing system had been laid out in the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and should 
provide fairer, faster and more equitable access to critical vaccines, treatments and tests during a 
pandemic, while driving innovation and growth in the pharmaceutical sector. The draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement showed what could be achieved when working together for the collective 
good and was testament to the importance of multilateralism. 

The representative of IRAQ expressed strong support for the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, which would be a cornerstone of international solidarity and shared responsibility. It 
sought to improve information sharing and ensure equity in and access to vaccines, medicines and 
medical equipment. His Government was committed to working with the Secretariat and Member 
States to ensure the effective and fair implementation of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, 
which should usher in a new era in which health was upheld as a fundamental human right. 

The representative of SWITZERLAND welcomed the conclusion of discussions on the main 
text of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement and noted the provisions on prevention, surveillance, 
the health workforce, regulatory systems and sustainable financing. Recognition in the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement of the One Health approach and the willingness of Member States to 
transfer technologies marked a step forward for health equity. The pathogen access and benefit-
sharing system must be effective and promote innovation. She therefore called for a pragmatic, 
voluntary approach that respected existing frameworks and took into consideration contributions 
from experts. 

The representative of BULGARIA said that, while she supported cross-sectoral cooperation to 
improve pandemic prevention, preparedness and response capabilities and acknowledged the 
benefits of working collectively at the international level, the imbalance of subject matter in the 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement was unfavourable and detrimental to Articles 4 and 5. 
Negotiations on Article 12, relating to the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system, had led to 
the inclusion of text that had not been fully discussed at the resumed thirteenth meeting of the 
Intergovernmental Negotiating Body. The lack of information on the forthcoming negotiations on 
the related annex gave rise to further uncertainty, including in terms of financial implications. The 
lack of a requirement for participants to have an expert profile and the shortened time frame for 
the drafting of the annex cast doubt on its quality and benefits. The work modalities of the 
Intergovernmental Negotiating Body were unacceptable. In view of those considerations, her 
Government would exercise its sovereign right once it had full information. 

The representative of LESOTHO welcomed the conclusion of negotiations on the draft WHO 
Pandemic Agreement and urged Member States to adopt the legally binding instrument. The draft 
WHO Pandemic Agreement represented a crucial step in addressing the gaps that the 
International Health Regulations (2005) could not fill, particularly in the areas of equitable access 
to health products, health workforce strengthening, sustainable financing and global supply chain 
resilience. As her country and the wider Region contributed to global disease surveillance yet were 
often without reciprocal access to medical countermeasures, she urged Member States to support 
the finalization and adoption of the annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system at 
the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly. 


Committee A: First meeting  17 

 

The representative of VANUATU recalled that the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement provided 
a historic opportunity to strengthen global health security, reinforce the role of WHO and ensure a 
timely, transparent and coordinated response to future health emergencies. The text of the draft 
WHO Pandemic Agreement reflected hard-won consensus forged through inclusive and 
constructive negotiations. He welcomed provisions in the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement that 
promoted equitable benefit sharing, regional manufacturing and health system resilience, 
particularly for low- and middle-income countries and small island developing States. He 
reaffirmed his support for WHO’s role as a multilateral organization and authority on health, 
including in global health emergencies. He supported the draft resolution and called on all 
Member States to pursue negotiations on the annex on the pathogen access and benefit-sharing 
system in the same spirit in which the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement had been negotiated. 

The representative of MEXICO commented on the importance of prevention, international 
scientific coordination, equitably strengthening international cooperation, and primary healthcare. 
The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement provided an opportunity to strengthen capacities and set out 
a normative framework that complemented the International Health Regulations (2005) and 
allowed for a coordinated global response to pandemics. She welcomed the inclusion in the draft 
WHO Pandemic Agreement of provisions to develop a pathogen access and benefit-sharing system 
that would promote equitable and timely access to vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics. The 
draft WHO Pandemic Agreement reflected the One Health approach and recognized the essential 
elements of gender equality, the protection of the health workforce and the right to development 
as fundamental to pandemic preparedness and response. The draft WHO Pandemic Agreement 
should be implemented in full, and inclusive governance mechanisms should be established to 
ensure the participation of citizens and patient groups in decision-making. 

The representative of HUNGARY emphasized the need to adopt the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement as a vital step towards stronger global pandemic prevention, preparedness and 
response. Any global health instrument must preserve the sovereign decision-making power of 
Member States, and her Government was proud to have contributed to the provisions of the draft 
WHO Pandemic Agreement that safeguarded national sovereignty. She looked forward to 
continued collaboration, including during negotiations on the annex on the pathogen access and 
benefit-sharing system. 

The representative of JAPAN commended the spirit of compromise within the 
Intergovernmental Negotiating Body and noted that the task of negotiating the annex on the 
pathogen access and benefit-sharing system remained. For a truly functional legal instrument, the 
system needed to be reasonable and viable both from scientific and economic perspectives in 
order to gain industry support. Expertise would be needed to ensure the successful conclusion of 
the negotiations. 

The representative of ISRAEL said that, while his Government had supported the process for 
developing the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement, it had proven difficult to reach consensus and 
the text presented therefore lacked clarity in many essential areas. He supported the remarks 
made by the representative of Bulgaria, noting that the proposed text referred to matters about 
which many Member States had expressed reservations, and other outstanding issues included 
the pathogen access and benefit-sharing system, patent rights and the budget. Many Member 
States had difficulty in accepting the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body’s proposed framework 
as a result. A way must be found to promote consensus. The text of the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, as proposed, was not suitable. He would welcome further evaluation of the text prior 
to its adoption. 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly  18 

 

The representative of BELGIUM expressed his conviction that the draft WHO Pandemic 
Agreement set out a strong foundation for further work and global cooperation to improve 
pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, and encouraged all Member States to support 
the draft resolution. Adoption of the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement would allow work to

Annex 

Best practices 

Elaboration of more specific standard criteria for the post of Regional Director 

1. Establishing more specific standard indicative criteria for the position of Regional Director 
would support the transparency, accountability and integrity of the election process by providing 
Member States of a region with information allowing for easier assessment of the relevant 
experience and education of candidates against a common standard, while preserving their ability 
to make a free choice among the candidates proposed. 

2. As the successful Regional Director candidate would assume a senior WHO staff position, 
consideration may be given, as appropriate, to using the criteria for appointment by WHO to a 
staff position at director level and above (D1/D2), accompanied by appropriate vetting, on an 
indicative basis. The D1/D2 criteria are: 

(a) a minimum of 15 years of relevant professional experience, including demonstrated 
experience at the international level – international experience is mandatory and means 
relevant experience gained outside the applicant’s home country; and 

(b) an advanced university degree relevant to the functions of the position. Only degrees 
from accredited institutions in the World Higher Education Database will be considered. 

3. In addition, existing criteria could be subject to further elaboration. This would provide 
further guidance for assessing candidates, and reference could be made to the WHO Values 
Charter, reflecting the values to which the WHO workforce is committed. Further, the Member 
State submitting the proposal could be asked to confirm that it has no knowledge of any ongoing 
or expected investigations and/or disciplinary/criminal/civil procedures, or any completed 
proceedings of this nature. 

4. The adoption of the measure(s) proposed above would require amendment to the regional 
committee rules of procedure. 

Formalization of live candidates’ forums 

5. All regional committees have held at least one live candidates’ forum. The formalization of 
live candidates’ forums that are broadcast to the public would support the transparency, 
accountability and integrity of the process by providing an opportunity for not only Member States 
but also the public and other interested parties to hear directly the views and goals of each 
candidate for the position of Regional Director. 

6. A regional committee adopting the practice of holding live candidates’ forums could also 
consider discontinuing the use of password-protected web forums (provided for in most of the 
codes of conduct for the nomination of Regional Directors) in favour of live forums. Recent 
experience shows relatively low levels of activity in web forums, while the human resources and 
technology costs of implementing and supporting them are relatively high. 


Resolutions and decisions  9 

 

7. To establish live candidates’ forums as a regular part of the nomination process, regional 
committees – other than those for Europe and the Americas – would need to amend their rules of 
procedure, as well as adopt modalities for live forums. The modalities could be modelled on 
existing forums, or alternatively, a different format could be followed; for example, a panel 
discussion whereby all candidates address the same questions. 

Broadcasting of interviews at regional committee meetings 

8. In the interests of transparency and accountability, where interviews of candidates are held 
at regional committee meetings,9 regional committees could consider amending the rules of 
procedure to permit the broadcasting of those interviews through a live stream. 

Amendment to codes of conduct 

9. Five of the six regional committees have adopted codes of conduct for the nomination of 
Regional Directors. Those regional committees could consider adopting revisions to enhance the 
nomination process, including by taking the following measures. 

(a) Expanded coverage: introduction of provisions for sexual misconduct and other 
abusive conduct, and a disclosure of interests by candidates, including with respect to 
tobacco and tobacco products and arms manufacturers. 

(b) Due diligence: provision for reference checks, such as ClearCheck and criminal record 
checks, and due diligence review of qualifications and employment history. 

(c) Strengthened disclosure of campaign activities: requesting nominating Member 
States to disclose grants or aid funding for candidates during the prior two years, and calling 
on non-nominating Member States to disclose such funding using a disclosure form 
prepared by the Secretariat. 

(d) Increased formality: requesting undertakings from candidates and nominating 
Member States regarding strict compliance with the relevant code of conduct. 

Establishment of a regional evaluation group 

10. A regional evaluation group could be established to play an advisory role in facilitating the 
robust assessment of candidates’ suitability and qualifications. The WHO European Region offers 
one model, but it is not the only approach. The respective regional committee may wish to 
consider the optimal composition of such a group, as well as its methodology and the range of 
tasks the group shall undertake. 

(a) Composition: the group would be composed of representatives of Member States of 
the region. The Secretariat could provide support and the group could consult with outside 
experts, as warranted. 

 

9 In the WHO European Region and in the WHO Region of the Americas, candidates are interviewed in advance 
of the respective regional committee meeting (by the Regional Evaluation Group, and at a meeting of the Regional 
Committee held on the margins of the Executive Committee, respectively). 


Executive Board, 157th session  10 

 

(b) Methodology: the group could evaluate candidates against the criteria set by the 
regional committee, through assessment of the information and documents submitted via 
standard forms for curriculum vitae, and/or through interview of candidates. 

(c) Role: the evaluation group could have an advisory role, providing a non-binding 
evaluation of candidates for consideration by the regional committee, and could, in the 
event that the number of candidates necessitates the creation of a shortlist, propose a 
recommended shortlist for consideration by the regional committee. 

11. The adoption of the measure(s) proposed above would require amendment to regional 
committee rules of procedure. 

Reopening of the election process under defined conditions 

12. Under the current election process, in most cases, the regional committees establish a 
shortlist of candidates and hold one or more secret ballots to select a single nominee. The 
Executive Board then considers that nominee on a yes/no basis. 

13. Consideration may be given to whether a regional committee should have the option to 
reopen the period for submitting proposals, should the field of candidates be considered 
insufficiently strong or representative. The regional evaluation group could be tasked with advising 
the regional committee on whether to exercise this power, or it could be triggered automatically 
in the event that a minimum number of candidates meeting the criteria is not proposed within the 
deadline. 

14. The adoption of the measure(s) proposed above would require amendment to regional 
committee rules of procedure.

3. An integral part of WHO’s oversight and accountability system, the independent, 
Organization-wide evaluation function produces high-quality evaluations informing  
evidence-based decision-making, strengthening accountability and transparency for results, 
facilitating organizational learning and enhancing performance. As such, evaluations inform the 
design and implementation of WHO’s and its partners’ health policies, programmes and budget 
priorities.  

4. The global context in which WHO operates has evolved considerably since 2018, with an 
increased focus on results that requires a stronger evaluation function to increase the 
Organization’s accountability, transparency and performance improvement through learning and 
use of evaluation recommendations. The world has experienced substantial changes and 
disruptions such as the pandemic of coronavirus disease (COVID-19) resulting in unacceptable 
impacts on human health and well-being across all countries and communities, more fragile 
national health systems and health emergency preparedness and response systems, and 
deepening country fiscal constraints, all resulting in significant reductions in progress towards the 
Sustainable Development Goals and greatly affecting the poorest and most vulnerable people. The 
rise in health and humanitarian emergencies, conflicts and crises poses considerable risks for 
global health.  

5. The critical role of evaluation in development is acknowledged in the 2030 Agenda for 
Sustainable Development,11 the United Nations General Assembly’s resolutions on 
capacity-building for the evaluation of development activities at the country level12 and on 
strengthening voluntary national reviews through country-led evaluation,13 the outcome of the 
2016 World Humanitarian Summit,14 and the resolution in 2020 on the quadrennial 
comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations 
system.15 These instruments provide new directions for the conduct of evaluation, including

Purpose 

7. The purpose of this policy is to define the overall framework for the independent evaluation 
function at WHO, its vision and goals, and to foster and enhance the culture and use of evaluation 
across the Organization, in adherence with best practices and with the norms and standards for 
evaluation of the United Nations Evaluation Group. The evaluation function supports WHO in 
achieving its core mandate and strategic priorities of its general programme of work, including its 
operational and normative roles. The policy guides the planning, conduct and use of evaluation 
findings and recommendations to strengthen organizational learning, accountability and 
evidence-based decision-making. Appendix 1 depicts the theory of change for the evaluation 
function. 

8. The WHO accountability framework embodies the “three lines of defence (assurance)” 
model19 with evaluation in the third line providing independent assurance critical for ensuring 
accountability, transparency and assessment of management effectiveness. Several types of 
assessments are included in the framework, all crucial to strengthening performance, 
accountability and institutional learning. This policy addresses only the assessments qualifying as 
“Evaluation” and excludes other forms of assessments conducted in WHO, such as audits, 
monitoring, reviews, performance assessment and surveys. 

Policy statement 

9. Evaluation is an essential independent function in WHO, carried out at all levels of the 
Organization. It ensures accountability and oversight for performance and results and reinforces 
organizational learning in order to inform evidence-based decision-making and support individual 
learning. The policy is applicable across the Organization and its operational contexts while 
affording necessary flexibility at the decentralized levels but still ensuring its independent 
functioning.  

Evaluation definition 

10. An evaluation is an assessment, conducted as systematically and impartially as possible, of 
an activity, project, programme, strategy, policy, topic, theme, sector, operational area or 
institutional performance. It analyses the level of achievement of both expected and unexpected 
results by examining the results chain, processes, contextual factors and causality using such 
appropriate criteria as relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, coherence and sustainability.

11. The independent evaluation function fosters evidence-based decision-making in the

accountability and learning systems and complies with United Nations’ evaluation principles, 
norms and standards while ensuring evaluations are independent, impartial, credible and useful

an essential part of WHO’s results-based management system that involves all aspects of the 
programme cycle: planning, prioritization, budgeting, managing the Organization toward results, 
monitoring and reporting results, evaluating performance – and using the knowledge and learning 
gained to feed into mid-course corrections, decisions and actions in pursuit of results. These 
functions are mutually supportive as they share a common goal, which is to help WHO to deliver

contributes to oversight in the Organization. While maintaining its independence and recognizing 
differentiated purposes and methods used, evaluation in WHO collaborates with other 
organizational oversight functions (such as audit, investigation, ethics and internal controls) as 
noted in the United Nations Evaluation Group’s norms and standards for evaluation.  

12. WHO has two broad categories of evaluation: 

(a) corporate evaluations, which are managed, commissioned or conducted by the 
Evaluation Office, and include thematic evaluations and programmatic evaluations; and 

(b) decentralized evaluations, which are managed, commissioned or conducted by 
divisions/ departments/offices in headquarters, regional offices or country offices other than

instances, the Evaluation Office provides quality assurance and technical backstopping. 

13. It should be noted that country programme evaluations can be commissioned by either 
country offices, regional offices or the Evaluation Office (described in paragraph 32(c)). In addition, 
WHO participates in and/or leads United Nations/multilateral inter-agency joint evaluations 
(see paragraph 34).

Impartiality 

15. The key elements of impartiality are objectivity, professional integrity and absence of bias. 
The requirement for impartiality exists at all stages of the evaluation process, including planning, 
formulating the mandate and scope, selecting the evaluation team, providing access to 
stakeholders, conducting the evaluation and formulating findings and recommendations. 

16. Evaluators need to be impartial, with the implication that evaluation team members must 
not have been (or expect to be in the near future) directly responsible for the policy-setting, 
design or management of the evaluation subject. 

Independence 

17. Independence of evaluation is necessary for credibility. It influences the ways in which an 
evaluation is used and allows evaluators to be impartial and free from undue pressure throughout 
the evaluation process. The independence of the evaluation function comprises three key aspects: 
behavioural, organizational and structural independence. As such, WHO is committed to 
safeguarding the independence and impartiality of all its evaluations. 

(a) Behavioural independence entails the ability to evaluate without undue influence by 
any party. Evaluators must have the full freedom to conduct their evaluative work 
impartially, without the risk of negative effects on their career development, and must be 
able to freely express their assessment. The independence of the evaluation function 
underpins the free access to information that evaluators should have on the evaluation 
subject. 

(b) Organizational independence requires that the central evaluation function is 
positioned independently from management functions, carries the responsibility of setting 
the evaluation agenda and is provided with adequate resources to conduct its work. 
Organizational independence also necessitates that evaluation managers have full discretion 
to directly submit evaluation reports to the appropriate level of decision-making and that 
they should report directly to an organization’s governing bodies and/or the executive head. 
Independence is vested in the Evaluation Office and in the Organization’s evaluation 
function to directly commission, produce, publish and disseminate duly quality-assured 
evaluation reports in the public domain without undue influence by any party. 

(c) Structural independence requires that the Evaluation Office has transparent view of 
and discretion and ability to manage its allocated budget and resources (staff and activity).  

18. Evaluators shall not be directly responsible for the policy, design or overall management of 
the subject under review. WHO staff members performing evaluations shall abide by the ethical 
principles for and standards of conduct of staff.24 External contractors shall abide by WHO’s

20. In commissioning and conducting an evaluation, there should be a clear intention to use the

organizational learning, informed decision-making processes and accountability for results.

21. Utility relates to the impact of the evaluation on decision-making and requires that 
evaluation findings be relevant and useful, presented in a clear and concise way, and monitored

of the programme and stakeholders, the credibility of the process and products, and the 
accessibility of reports.  

22. Utility will be ensured through: 

(a) the systematic prioritizing of the evaluation agenda based on established criteria and 
consultation with relevant stakeholders; 

(b) inclusion in an evaluation’s terms of reference of provisions for timely commissioning

users; 

(c) requirement for a management response to be produced within 60 days of completion 
of evaluation;  

(d) the systematic follow-up, monitoring and reporting of recommendations and 
management responses;  

(e) the systematic use of evaluations’ findings and recommendations for evidence-based 
decision-making to design and implement policies, strategies, programmes/projects and 
budgets; 

(f) public access to evaluation products; and  

(g) alignment with the results-based management framework.

Credibility 

23. Evaluations must be credible. Credibility is grounded on impartiality, independence and a 
rigorous methodology. Key elements of credibility include transparent evaluation processes, 
inclusive approaches involving relevant stakeholders and robust quality assurance systems. 
Evaluation results (or findings) and recommendations are derived from – or informed by – the 
conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the best available, objective, reliable and valid data and 
by accurate quantitative and qualitative analysis of evidence. Credibility requires that evaluations 
are ethically conducted and managed by evaluators that exhibit professional and cultural 
competencies.27 

Quality 

24. Quality relates to the appropriate and accurate use of evaluation criteria, impartial 
presentation and analysis of evidence, and coherence between findings, conclusions and 
recommendations.  

25. Quality will be ensured through: 

(a) the continuous adherence to evaluation methodology as elaborated in WHO’s 
evaluation guidance documents and the applicable guidelines and the norms and standards 
for evaluation of the United Nations Evaluation Group; and 

(b) a comprehensive quality assurance system, including independent quality assessments 
for evaluation processes and products and annual reporting on the quality of all corporate 
and decentralized evaluations.  

26. The Evaluation Office supports the three levels of the Organization by providing quality 
assurance for evaluations undertaken. In addition, regional evaluation officers provide quality 
assurance for evaluations undertaken at the country and regional levels, along with the Evaluation 
Office as needed.  

Transparency 

27. Transparency is an essential element of evaluation that establishes trust and builds 
confidence, enhances stakeholder ownership and increases public accountability. Evaluation 
products should be publicly accessible.28 

28. To achieve transparency, stakeholders should be aware of the reason for the evaluation, the 
selection criteria and the purposes for which the findings will be used. Transparency of process is 
also important, as is the accessibility of evaluation materials and products.  

29. Transparency will be ensured through the approaches described in this policy. The 
commissioner of the evaluation will ensure a continuous consultation process with relevant 
stakeholders at all stages of the evaluation process. The evaluation report shall contain details of 
evaluation methodologies, approaches, sources of information and costs incurred. In accordance

Ethics 

30. Evaluation must be conducted with the highest standards of integrity and respect for the 
beliefs, manners and customs of the social and cultural environment; for human rights and gender 
equality; and for the “do no harm” principle for humanitarian assistance. Evaluators must respect 
the rights of institutions and individuals to provide information in confidence, must ensure that 
sensitive data are protected and cannot be traced to their source and must validate statements 
made in the report with those who provided the relevant information. Evaluators should obtain 
informed consent for the use of private information from those who provide it. When evidence of 
wrongdoing is uncovered, it must be reported discreetly to a competent WHO body (such as the 
relevant office of internal oversight).29

31. The universally recognized values and principles of human rights and gender equality need 
to be integrated into all stages of an evaluation. It is the responsibility of evaluators and evaluation 
managers to ensure that these values are respected, addressed and promoted, underpinning the 
commitment to the principle of “no one left behind”.30,31 Pursuant to the United Nations 
Evaluation Group’s guidance on integrating disability inclusion in evaluations and reporting on the 
United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy entity accountability framework (2022)32 and on 
integrating human rights and gender equality in evaluations (2024), and the WHO policy on

Planning and prioritization of evaluations 

36. WHO will develop a biennial, Organization-wide evaluation workplan, including indicative 
costing and funding sources, for corporate and decentralized evaluations as part of the 
Organization’s planning and budgeting cycle. These shall be submitted to the Executive Board for 
approval through the Programme, Budget and Administration Committee. The Secretariat will also 
update the biennial workplan, as needed, in the annual report to the Programme, Budget and 
Administration Committee and the Executive Board. The approved workplan will be implemented 
by inclusion in the Organization’s programme budget and operational planning processes, 
including regional and country office workplans as well as costing and resource allocation, and 
results monitoring. 

37. The workplan shall be established in consultation with senior management at headquarters 
and regional offices and with heads of WHO country offices, with feedback from the Independent 
Expert Oversight Advisory Committee, based on established coverage norms, strategic priorities 
and selection and prioritization criteria (requirement, utility and significance).  

38. The following categories shall be considered in the development of criteria for the selection 
of topics for evaluation:  

(a) organizational requirement relevant to: requests from governing bodies (decisions, 
resolutions, approved strategies or policies); global, international or regional commitments; 
and specific agreements with stakeholders, partners or donors; 

(b) organizational significance relating to: strategic priorities of the general programme of 
work and core functions; level of investment; risks identified in the principal risks and risk 
registers; recurrent issues emerging from evaluations and internal and external audits; 
performance issues or concerns in relation to achievements of expected results; country 
cooperation strategies (if selected) at the middle or penultimate year of the period of a 
strategy; and 

(c) organizational utility relating to: a cross-cutting issue, theme, programme or policy 
question; potential for staff or institutional learning and/or innovation; and degree of 
comparative advantage of WHO. 

Additional selection criteria will include ensuring minimum coverage norms. 

Coverage norms 

39. The biennial evaluation workplan should ensure adequate coverage of evaluations across 
the Organization and categories in order to provide a representative, unbiased picture of WHO’s 
contribution to achievement of results, and ensure that policies, strategies and programmes are 
evidence-based (see Appendix 2). The design of new strategies, programmes and country 
strategies must be informed by an adequate and relevant body of evaluations.  

40. Minimum coverage for corporate and decentralized evaluations at the country, regional and 
headquarter levels, along with responsibilities for evaluation management and indicative funding 
sources, is presented in Appendix 2. In addition, various organizational levels and entities 
commissioning evaluations have the flexibility to prioritize topics, interventions and timing in line 
with their policy or programme cycles and stakeholder needs.

Internal WHO alignment and efficiencies 

41. As a core part of the results-based management function, evaluation is key to and 
interlinked with the Organization’s planning, prioritization, budget, results monitoring and 
reporting and learning cycle. As such, evaluation will align with and be complementary to the 
respective managerial and enabling functions across the Organization. 

42. Evaluation works closely and collaboratively with other oversight/accountability and 
enabling functions, such as audit, ethics and legal. In addition, evaluation is one of several distinct 
yet complementary functions, including audit, research, monitoring, data and analytics and 
organizational learning that together form an evidence ecosystem. Though functionally 
independent, the evaluation function is committed to maximizing efficiencies and cooperating 
with all these functions in a whole-of-organization manner wherever appropriate and feasible, 
notably in coordinating development of respective workplans to avoid concurrent or duplicative 
reviews of the same entity and conducting analyses of root causes and identifying ways to 
enhance WHO’s business case and value added. 

43. Even as it seeks to actively collaborate, evaluation must retain its independence. Through 
leadership, joint work planning and funding and capacity strengthening, the Evaluation Office will 
ensure full coherence with the decentralized evaluation function including in regional and 
country offices. 

Risks 

44. Successfully planning and implementing biennial evaluation workplans across the 
Organization will consider the Organization’s principal risks, risk management strategy, risk 
appetite framework, risk register and planned mitigation measures. Additional risks can vary 
across the Organization, such as political sensitivity, evaluator availability or absorption capacity. 
The Evaluation Office will develop and monitor mitigating measures for identified  
Organization-wide risks for the evaluation function; with each level of the Organization tailoring 
mitigation strategies for their respective risks. Risks are also reflected in the assumptions included 
in the theory of change (see Appendix 1). These include the organizational context in which the 
function operates (for example: independence; effective results-based management systems; 
enabling environment for evaluation; organizational leadership; ownership and support; and 
incentives for evaluations and their use), resources (for example, adequate and predictable 
financial and human resources commensurate with needs), and governing bodies’ and partners’ 
demand for evaluations.

document JIU/REP/2014/6, p. 29 (accessed 25 April 2025). 

38 Document PBAC41/2, paragraph 28.

(accessed 25 April 2025). 

https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/development-co-operation-evaluation-and-effectiveness/evaluation-criteria.html


Executive Board, 157th session  26 

 

towards this target. Consequently, based on a clear taxonomy for evaluations, the Organization 
will progressively strive to increase allocation of its expenditure for the evaluation function over 
the next two bienniums towards international benchmarks. 

51. Two mechanisms commonly used in other United Nations entities and bilateral aid 
organizations are: (a) a dedicated programme/project budget line (proposals and donor 
agreements) for evaluation; and (b) pooled resources within the Organization to support the 
evaluation function and to promote and ensure independence. With expected growth in 
evaluation coverage and required resources needed, particularly at the regional and country office 
levels, specific strategies will be developed to reach the WHO evaluation coverage norms drawing 
from various sources (including voluntary contributions and/or pooled funding) and learning from 
innovations in the United Nations system and emerging good practices adapted to WHO’s context 
as appropriate. An immediate option is to use the common practice of having programme 
evaluation budget line items (as agreed) and requiring set-asides for evaluations of large 
programmes or projects (for example, more than US$ 10 million life-of-project, or less as desired). 

52. The Evaluation Office, in collaboration with other organizational entities, will routinely 
monitor expenditures for conducting and managing evaluations across the Organization, and 
include its findings in the evaluation annual report to the Executive Board. 

Human resources and organizational capacity 

53. In order to strengthen the evaluation function and culture across the three levels of the 
Organization, a cadre of evaluation professionals (corporate and regional evaluation officers) with 
harmonized competencies, clearly defined roles and responsibilities, and alignment with 
results-based management structures and managerial responsibilities is required. Primary 
responsibilities include leading evaluation activities, supporting decentralized40 evaluations 
whenever relevant and/or requested, serving as the focal point for planning decentralized 
evaluations and country programme evaluations in their respective regions in line with the United 
Nations Evaluation Group’s norms and standards and provisions for impartiality and independence 
set out above. Regional evaluation officers support their respective Regional Directors and 
regional committees, as requested, by providing updates on evaluation workplans and lessons 
derived from recommendations. 

54. To promote the culture and practice of evaluation across WHO, the Evaluation Office, in 
collaboration with regional offices, facilitates development and implementation of  
Organization-wide capacity strengthening for all evaluation staff members involved in the 
commissioning, management and implementation of recommendations of evaluations, including 
use of shared competency frameworks, learning pathways and programmes and tailored training. 
The Evaluation Office facilitates an Organization-wide Global Network on Evaluation to: engage all 
evaluation staff members in capacity development; share information and learning; participate in 
the preparation of the biennial Organization-wide evaluation workplan; facilitate development 
and tracking of management responses; contribute to the annual report on evaluation; and advise 
programmes across WHO on evaluation issues, as needed. Additional training/capacity 
development will be developed to orient and increase evaluation understanding for and practice 
by programme officers, particularly at the country office level and in humanitarian or fragile 
contexts. 

 

40 Evaluations not conducted by the Evaluation Office or by regional office evaluation officers.

https://www.unjiu.org/sites/www.unjiu.org/files/jiu_document_files/products/en/reports-notes/JIU%20Products/JIU_REP_2014_6_English.pdf

Annex 3  27 

 

Accountability and oversight within WHO 

55. Within the WHO accountability framework there are clear definitions on from whom, and to 
whom authority flows and for what purpose including for the evaluation function. It further 
defines the accountability of those with authority and their responsibility in exercising that 
authority. The evaluation policy defines the specific roles and responsibilities of the main actors in 
the evaluation process as well as the mechanism used to monitor implementation of the 
evaluation policy including across the three levels of the Organization. 

56. The Director-General, Regional Directors, senior management, directors and heads of 
country offices across the Organization play a critical role in, and share accountability for, 
promoting a culture of evaluation, ensuring the implementation of this policy, including its 
coverage, resourcing and use, while upholding United Nations Evaluation Group’s norms and 
standards, particularly by safeguarding evaluation independence. 

Roles and responsibilities 

57. The Executive Board of WHO41 will: 

(a) approve the revised WHO evaluation policy (2025) and subsequent amendments, as 
needed;  

(b) provide oversight of the evaluation function within the Organization and ensure that 
the evaluation function is duly independent;  

(c) encourage the use of credible and independent evaluation evidence as an input to 
strategic planning and decision-making;  

(d) provide input to the biennial Organization-wide evaluation workplan on the items of 
specific interest to Member States;  

(e) approve the biennial Organization-wide evaluation workplan, including its indicative 
budget and ensuring adequate resourcing;  

(f) consider and take note of the annual report of the implementation of the biennial 
Organization-wide evaluation workplan; and  

(g) periodically revise the evaluation policy, as necessary. 

58. As part of its terms of reference,42 the Independent Expert Oversight Advisory Committee 
reviews the evaluation function for WHO as a whole and provides advice to the Executive Board 
through the Programme, Budget and Administration Committee. Areas of guidance include the 
staffing, resources and performance of the evaluation function, including provision of advice to 
the Director-General on the selection and performance of the Director, Evaluation and on the 
biennial workplan for evaluation activities, and monitoring the timely, effective and appropriate 
implementation of all evaluation recommendations. The Committee further provides guidance on 
implementing the evaluation policy, particularly regarding the Evaluation Office’s role in 

 

41 And its subsidiary organ: the Programme, Budget and Administration Committee. 

42 See document EB150/5, Annex and summary records of the 150th session of the Executive Board, 
twelfth meeting, section 1 (document EB150/REC/2/2022). 


Executive Board, 157th session  28 

 

strengthening oversight and accountability, promoting learning and improving the Organization’s 
responsiveness to evaluations. 

59. The Evaluation Office is the custodian of the evaluation function and reports directly to the 
Director-General and reports to the Executive Board annually on matters relating to evaluation at 
WHO. The Office is responsible for the following functions:  

(a) safeguarding the independence and impartiality of the evaluation function in line with 
the United Nations Evaluation Group’s norms and standards; 

(b) leading the development of a biennial Organization-wide evaluation workplan;  

(c) informing senior management about evaluation-related issues of Organization-wide 
importance;  

(d) facilitating the input and use of evaluation findings and lessons learned for strategic 
decision-making, programme planning and organizational learning;  

(e) coordinating the implementation of the framework for evaluation across the three 
levels of the Organization;  

(f) collaborating, as appropriate, with other oversight functions (for example, audit) to 
ensure complementarity and coherence while upholding independence; 

(g) developing key performance indicators and monitoring compliance across the 
Organization with the policy;  

(h) mobilizing sustainable financial support for all evaluations in the Organization from 
internal and external sources (voluntary and assessed contributions), partners and 
stakeholders through voluntary contributions; 

(i) developing, disseminating and facilitating use of guidance for management responses 
to evaluations (for business owners) and for maintaining a system to track follow-up;  

(j) ensuring that all evaluations conducted in the Organization include an evaluation 
reference and/or management group that throughout the evaluation process provides 
guidance, review and input into the scope and methodology to be used and draft reports, 
and ensures that all processes are followed according to the WHO evaluation policy; the 
group will not interfere with the work of the independent evaluators; 

(k) upholding ethical standards in evaluation, including informed consent, confidentiality 
and safeguarding of vulnerable populations;  

(l) maintaining a publicly available inventory of evaluations performed across WHO to 
enhance knowledge sharing and institutional memory;  

(m) maintaining a roster of experts and entities with evaluation experience;  

(n) providing guidance material and advice for the preparation, conduct and follow-up of 
evaluations, including promoting participatory approaches in evaluation planning and 
implementation by engaging relevant stakeholders across all levels;  


Annex 3  29 

 

(o) reviewing evaluation reports on compliance with the requirements of the policy, and 
ensuring quality of evaluation processes and deliverables;  

(p) strengthening capacities in evaluation among WHO professional evaluation staff 
members (for example, making available standardized methodologies or training on 
evaluation), as well as awareness-raising materials for all business owners;  

(q) submitting an annual report on corporate and decentralized evaluation activities to the 
Executive Board; and  

(r) supporting the periodic review of and updates to the policy as needed. 

60. The Director-General shall appoint a technically qualified Director of the Evaluation Office 
after consultation with the Executive Board. The Director-General shall likewise consult the Board 
before any termination of the incumbent of that office. The Director of the Evaluation Office 
serves for a fixed term of four years with a possibility of reappointment only once for a further 
term of four years and is barred from re-entry into the Organization after the expiry of their term.  

Use of evaluation findings 

61. Recommendations contained in evaluation reports reflect the value added by the evaluation 
process. Each evaluation shall have an identified owner, such as the responsible officer of a 
division, department, programme, office or project. It is the responsibility of the owner to use the 
findings of the evaluation and develop an action plan for implementing the recommendations. 

62. Evaluations improve organizational learning and performance by requiring that the object 
and intent of and alignment with the general programme of work and organizational goals be clear 
at the outset before their being commissioned or conducted. Evaluations should also align with 
the results and impact frameworks of the general programme of work and with the programme 
budget and take into account progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals. At the 
country level, this requirement involves aligning evaluations with the country office’s strategic 
planning cycle, governmental planning timelines, advocacy initiatives and WHO’s planning and 
budgeting processes.  

Management responses 

63. To maximize accountability and use of evaluation recommendations and lessons learned in 
decision-making in a timely fashion, the evaluation owner will ensure that a management 
response is issued within two months of completion of a given evaluation. Following approval by 
senior management (namely the Office of the Director-General or relevant Assistant 
Director-General at headquarters, or by the Regional Director or Director, Programme 
Management for the regional and country offices), management responses are published on the 
WHO website to ensure transparency.  

64. The Director-General, in collaboration with Regional Directors, will establish a mechanism to 
ensure effective follow-up and monitoring of the implementation of evaluation recommendations 
in a systematic manner, coordinating efforts with the evaluation owners. Senior management will 
review the status of implementation progress for management responses on at least a biannual 
basis. Use of the Consolidated Platform for Recommendation Tracking and its dashboard along 
with status reports on progress in the implementation of the recommendations will be submitted 
as part of the evaluation annual report to the Executive Board through the Programme, Budget 


Executive Board, 157th session  30 

 

and Administration Committee. Continuous monitoring and reporting of follow-up to 
recommendations are key to enhancing the use of evaluations for learning and accountability 
purposes. 

Organizational learning 

65. The Evaluation Office and regional offices will increase their capacity to respond proactively 
to knowledge needs of the Organization and develop mechanisms to foster timely 
Organization-wide sharing of learning.  

66. The Evaluation Office along with regional offices will synthesize evidence of completed 
evaluations and conduct cross-cutting analyses of evaluation findings/conclusions, 
recommendations and their implementation to identify emerging trends, root causes and 
potential solutions. It will increase the utility of evaluations to nurture dialogue with policy-makers 
and programme decision-makers. Results of evaluation synthesis reports will be submitted to the 
Executive Board and made publicly available. 

67. The Evaluation Office, in collaboration with regional offices, will develop an 
Organization-wide and management-driven learning agenda and plan focused on crucial questions 
affecting the achievement of organizational results. It will also collaborate with global, regional 
and country communities of evaluation practice. 

68. In addition to further strengthening learning within WHO, the evaluation function will 
enhance the global knowledge base by sharing evaluation evidence with the United Nations 
Evaluation Group, other United Nations entities, evaluation stakeholders and partners, as well as 
Member States, think-tanks, the academic community, the research community and communities 
of practice.  

Disclosure and dissemination of evaluation reports 

69. All evaluations should have a plan for dissemination of their reports at the outset to further 
bolster evaluation use.  

70. Evaluation reports, related products and their management responses will be made publicly 
available in accordance with the Organization’s disclosure policy. These documents will be widely 
disseminated to ensure public access and to enhance visibility so as to promote greater awareness 
and use of their recommendations. Communication channels and means to increase transparency 
include, but are not limited to, informal information sessions for Member States, digital platforms 
and Internet pages, dashboards on the WHO Member States portal, as well as social media, 
webinars, newsletters, podcasts and specific targeting. 

71. Lessons learned from evaluations will be distilled, reported and disseminated as appropriate. 

Communication of the policy 

72. This policy will be disseminated across the Organization along with complementary guidance 
to ensure its meaningful and consistent implementation. The Evaluation Office will draw up and 
implement a communication plan which will be championed by senior management to strengthen 
the evaluation culture across the three levels of the Organization and develop a common 
understanding of WHO evaluation policy standards, expectations and potential use. 


Annex 3  31 

 

Monitoring and evaluation
