monitored by the Independent Expert Oversight Advisory Committee and the Secretariat and

EB156(14) Strengthening national capacities in evidence-based decision-
making for the uptake and impact of norms and standards22 

The Executive Board, having considered the report by the Director-General,23 

Decided to recommend to the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly the adoption of the 
following resolution: 

The Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, 

Having considered the report by the Director-General; 

Recalling the collective commitment to achieve universal health coverage and the role 
of evidence, knowledge and innovation in promoting quality of care, improving financial 
protection and driving positive outcomes; 

Recognizing WHO’s unique status as a science- and evidence-based organization and 
its normative leadership, as outlined in its Constitution and in the Fourteenth General 
Programme of Work, 2025–2028, with its renewed focus on country-level impact including 
through timely delivery, expanded access to and uptake of WHO’s normative, technical and 
data products; 

Recalling the experiences encountered during the pandemic of coronavirus disease 
(COVID-19) and the need for robust and timely clinical and public health guidance that is 
relevant to context and responsive to local needs and equity considerations;

Recognizing scientific evidence as an important basis for the development of clinical 
and public health guidance; and recognizing also the value of science and high-quality 
evidence in ensuring that complex information is synthesized and available in accessible 
formats for end-users to guide practice and improve health outcomes; 

Concerned that there are significant gaps, including inadequate resources, in the 
capacity of countries to produce and use relevant local and global evidence in developing 
new clinical and public health guidelines or in adapting existing guidelines with proper 
feedback systems to measure the cost-effectiveness and quality of clinical care, public health 
guidance and policy and their impact on population health and well-being; 

Recalling the Constitution of the World Health Organization, resolution  
WHA75.8 (2022) on strengthening clinical trials to provide high-quality evidence on health 
interventions and to improve research quality and coordination, and resolution  
WHA63.21 (2010) on WHO’s role and responsibilities in health research; 

Acknowledging the recommendations from the external evaluation on WHO’s 
normative function at the country level that address the impact and effectiveness of WHO’s 
normative products within individual country context;24 

Emphasizing the critical role of evidence-based WHO norms and standards in health 
decision-making and the need to maintain trust in the health system and the global health 
processes for establishing norms and standards, especially in the light of misinformation and 
disinformation; 

Underlying the need to foster strong local and regional clinical and public health 
leadership and innovation that are human-centred and based on science and evidence, 
which is the key to creating a conducive environment for local investment in research, public 
health infrastructure and other supportive systems at local and regional levels; 

Acknowledging the importance of supporting local priorities and informing  
context-specific research, including through implementation research, local innovation and 
product development for priority diseases that include ongoing efforts, such as those on 
proven approaches focusing on quality vaccines, diagnostics, therapeutics, medical supplies 
and including nonpharmacological, digital, public health and prevention interventions, 

1. URGES Member States,25 in accordance with national contexts: 

(1) to institutionalize, as appropriate, structures, systems and processes for the 
development and adaptation of clinical and public health guidance; 

(2) to strengthen national quality control, as well as regulatory frameworks and 
authorities, to facilitate appropriate uptake of global clinical and public health 
recommendations; 

(3) to enhance and sustain investment to strengthen national capability for guideline 
adaptation and timely uptake of normative products, including fit-for-purpose digital 
technologies that are tailored to public health needs and their respective health 
system maturity levels;

Recognizing that some persons living with a rare disease have disabilities, which may 
have a greater impact on their health, and that they may also face various barriers, which 
may hinder their full and effective participation in society on an equal basis with others;31 

Recognizing also that, in addition to the physical impact, some persons living with a 
rare disease, their families and caregivers may experience discrimination and psychosocial 
consequences, such as isolation, stigmatization and limited opportunities for social inclusion, 
which are often intensified by a lack of public awareness and knowledge and the absence, 
limited scope or poor implementation of policies and social support; 

Recognizing further that persons living with a rare disease (including those whose 
disease is undiagnosed), their families and caregivers may be psychologically, socially and 
economically vulnerable throughout their life course, facing specific challenges in several 
areas, including but not limited to physical and mental health, education, employment, 
financial well-being and leisure; 

Emphasizing the importance of adopting a holistic patient-centred approach to address 
the needs of persons living with a rare disease, focusing on enhancing their functioning and 
working with society to remove, to the extent possible, the barriers they face in accessing 
health, education, employment and other domains of life; 

Noting that the high prices of many health products for rare diseases, and inequitable 
access to such products within and among countries, as well as the financial hardships 
associated with their high costs pose significant challenges for some persons living with a 
rare disease; 

Recognizing from an equity perspective that women and children living with a rare 
disease encounter greater challenges in accessing care, including the late diagnosis, biases in 
symptom assessment and reduced access to timely and appropriate treatment, which 
significantly impact their quality of life and overall health outcomes; 

Recognizing also the importance of achieving universal health coverage, including for 
persons living with a rare disease and their families and caregivers, and that universal health 
coverage implies that all people have access, without discrimination, to nationally 
determined sets of essential quality health services, from health promotion to disease 
prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care, as well as essential, safe, 
affordable, effective and quality medicines, vaccines, diagnostics and health technologies, 
including assistive technologies, ensuring that the cost of using these services does not lead 
to financial hardship; 

Recognizing further the importance of implementing integrated care, considering the 
health system along with social and community services, for enabling persons living with a 
rare disease to achieve optimal health and well-being; 

Acknowledging that to enhance physical and mental health, well-being and life 
expectancy for everyone, it is essential to achieve universal health coverage, including 
persons living with a rare disease;

procurement of cost-effective commodities, with a focus on leaving no one behind, 


Executive Board, 156th session  26 

 

 

and that support better coordination, collaboration and alignment of partners, 
regional and international institutions in providing long-term, reliable support; 

(5) to strengthen and elevate WHO’s existing, dedicated observatory function to 
monitor and report on development assistance and domestic financing flows for health 
in order to increase the visibility and transparency of financing and financial protection 
trends in terms of volume and efficiency, assess and evaluate their impact and 
generate knowledge and expertise, leveraging the national health accounts and other 
sources of data and boosting regional and country-level capacity and leadership on 
health financing to support developing countries, in partnership with United Nations 
organizations, international development partners, international financial institutions, 
foundations, academic institutions, civil society organizations and other stakeholders, 
in line with the Framework of Engagement with Non-State Actors, as applicable; 

(6) to provide support, as requested by Member States, for the development of 
prioritized national health financing road maps to mobilize technical assistance and 
financial resources in order to strengthen national health financing systems and to 
improve the coordination and collaboration of development partners, United Nations 
entities, international financial institutions including the World Bank, civil society, and 
the private sector, in line with the Framework of Engagement with Non-State Actors, 
as applicable. 

(Eighteenth meeting, 10 February 2025) 

EB156(17) Strengthening medical imaging capacity45 

The Executive Board, having considered the report by the Director-General,46 

Decided to recommend to the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly the adoption of the 
following resolution: 

The Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, 

Having considered the report by the Director-General; 

Recognizing that medical imaging is vital for the diagnosis and treatment of numerous 
communicable diseases, noncommunicable diseases, traumatic injuries and other health 
conditions, including gastrointestinal and gynaecological conditions; 

Considering that medical imaging requires traceable, cost-effective medical technology 
with consumables and accessories, an associated trained health workforce, knowledge of 
clinical procedures, patient information, affordable access, patient management, patient 
preparation, interpretation and reporting; 

Recognizing that medical imaging for diagnosis and treatment, both conventional as 
well as interventional, refers to medical devices using ionizing radiation (such as 
computerized tomography scanners and positron emission tomography (PET)), non-ionizing 

 

45 See Annex 8 for the financial and administrative implications for the Secretariat of this decision. 

46 Document EB156/6. 


Resolutions and decisions 27 

 

 

radiation (such as ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)) and hybrid imaging 
modalities (such as PET-MRI); 

Noting that the optimal use of medical imaging services in many countries is affected 
by, inter alia, the limited availability of affordable and cost-effective medical imaging 
technologies, reduced access in remote and rural areas, the shortage of a trained health 
workforce and the lack of effective or implementable policies, plans and guidelines; 

Highlighting the need to improve equitable access to safe and effective medical 
imaging globally, particularly to enhance detection, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and 
understanding of both communicable and noncommunicable diseases;47 

Noting that the burden of cancer and other noncommunicable diseases is rising and 
recognizing that medical imaging is essential for appropriate cancer detection and therapy, 
including surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy; 

Acknowledging that in 2021 of all neurological conditions stroke was the leading cause 
of disability-adjusted life years, with the largest burden on developing countries; 

Confirming that medical imaging can contribute to reductions in mortality, morbidity 
and incidence through early detection and monitoring of many neurological conditions such 
as multiple sclerosis, nervous system cancers, neurodegenerative disorders48 and stroke, 
including through rapidly distinguishing between haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke and 
determining treatment such as thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy; 

Taking into account that equitable access to medical imaging for early diagnosis and 
management can reduce lifelong consequences from infectious diseases that contribute to 
global morbidity and mortality, with particular emphasis on individuals at risk especially 
among those in vulnerable situations and those that are hard to reach; 

Noting that accurate medical imaging can minimize unnecessary surgical interventions 
and optimize complex medical interventions; 

Recognizing that medical imaging is essential in emergencies, road traffic crashes and 
disasters, enabling emergency medical responders to quickly assess injuries, identify critical 
conditions and prioritize care, and can aid surgical interventions including for traumatic brain 
and spinal cord injuries;

1. Opening of the session and adoption of the agenda: Item 1 of the provisional agenda

Opening of the session 

The CHAIR declared open the 156th session of the Executive Board. 

Adoption of the agenda 

The CHAIR said that the Executive Board was meeting at a time when global health 
governance was under scrutiny, multilateralism under threat and the climate crisis unrelenting, all 
of which heightened geopolitical tensions and conflict, posing risks to global health. 
Misinformation and disinformation on public health challenges affected the credibility of WHO 
and its ability to build consensus on and implement global health policy. The funding of WHO’s 
global agenda demanded the Organization’s full attention and required creativity to develop 
innovative means of financing. Since decisions made at the current session of the Executive Board 
would have an impact on the future of WHO as an institution, on global health governance and on 
the health of billions across the world, it was important to focus on concrete deliverables ensuring 
that the Organization was fit for purpose, sustainably financed and agile enough to address its 
programme of work and any health emergencies.  

Presenting a summary of the previous day’s informal meeting, he said that the participants 
had discussed critical issues; the notification by the United States of America of its intention to 
withdraw from the Organization, governance reform, and agenda and resolution management, 
particularly the financial implications of draft resolutions. They had also discussed strategic 
matters, such as the development of the Proposed programme budget 2026–2027 and the 
increase in assessed contributions, which had been supported by the Programme, Budget and 
Administration Committee of the Executive Board. There was a common understanding of the 
current difficult financial situation, in response to which WHO would pursue the twin goals of 
resource mobilization and efficiency gains. The need for WHO to improve communication 
activities had also been also highlighted. 

He drew attention to the Secretariat’s proposal to delete items 23.3 (Scale of assessments 
2026–2027 [if any]), 23.4 (Amendments to the Financial Regulations and Financial Rules [if any]) 
and 26.2 (Independent Expert Oversight Advisory Committee: membership renewal [if any]), as 
there were no matters to discuss under those items. He took it that the Board agreed to that 
proposal. 

It was so agreed.

future general agreement between WHO and the European Union, the European Union attended

It was so agreed. 

The UNITED NATIONS DEPUTY DIRECTOR-GENERAL said that, at a time when the world was 
facing global threats, geopolitical tensions, deepening inequalities, climate shocks and the erosion 
of multilateralism, the United Nations system stood in support of WHO and its mandate. Global 
health needs were expanding while already diminished resources were being stretched. Against 
that backdrop, WHO, as the guardian of global health, was working constantly, responding to 
disease outbreaks, mobilizing resources for conflict-related activities, deploying life-saving 
resources and providing unparalleled technical expertise where it was needed most. There was 
much more to do, however, and the outcomes of certain 2023 high-level meetings of the General 
Assembly had strengthened collective resolve, resulting in, inter alia, the Pact for the Future. The 
United Nations development system would play a critical role in implementation of global 
commitments in order to see action on the ground. With the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable 
Development Goals fast approaching, action must be taken to build strong health systems, 
thereby investing in a healthy and safe world for generations to come. 

2. Report by the Director-General: Item 2 of the agenda (document EB156/2) 

The DIRECTOR-GENERAL outlined the Organization’s achievements on multiple fronts in 
2024: delivering an impact at the country level; supporting countries in developing systems to 
protect their populations from climate risks and introducing universal health coverage; expanding 
health services during humanitarian crises; improving access to medicines; and strengthening 
regulatory authorities around the world. Other achievements related to initiatives to reduce 
smoking and tobacco use, improve diets, prevent obesity, counter antimicrobial resistance, 
eliminate diseases, promote mental health among young people and maintain the momentum to 
address maternal and child mortality. 

WHO had also responded to various health emergencies around the world, including by 
delivering millions of dollars’ worth of supplies, and to insecurity in areas of conflict, for example 
by meeting acute health needs and supporting the operation of hospitals in the Gaza Strip. Attacks 
on healthcare were becoming the “new normal” in conflicts, and he urged Member States to 
implement the recommendations published by WHO for bringing to account those responsible for 
attacks on healthcare. Drawing on the lessons learned during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) 
pandemic, WHO had strengthened its work in every dimension of emergency prevention, 
preparedness and response, monitoring developments of outbreaks, and scanning the world for

public health threats. Further to a 2024 review, the Organization’s transformation process had 
been reprioritized and realigned with the priorities of the Fourteenth General Programme of 
Work, 2025–2028. 

He regretted the announcement by the United States of America that it intended to 
withdraw from WHO and hoped that the decision would be reconsidered. In response to the main 
reasons cited for the withdrawal, he observed that the Organization had implemented the deepest 
and most wide-ranging reforms in its history, including the recommendations of the Action for 
Results Group to strengthen WHO country offices. It had addressed the imbalance between 
assessed and voluntary contributions, and its overreliance on a handful of traditional donors. It 
had activated its emergency incident management system even before the first COVID-19 death 
had been reported in China, and, in response to the multiple independent reviews of the global 
response to the pandemic, had taken steps, together with Member States, to strengthen global 
health security. As a United Nations agency, WHO was impartial and existed to serve all countries 
and all people. Even before the announcement by the United States of America, the Organization 
had been contending with a financing shortfall due to the economic difficulties faced by many 
countries and had been working to simultaneously mobilize new resources and reduce 
expenditure. In the face of the current more acute situation, it had introduced a set of measures 
to protect its workforce and enable it to continue carrying out its duties. 

The representative of BRAZIL reaffirmed his country’s support for multilateralism and 
emphasized the need for sustainable and predictable funding for WHO. It was essential to 
prioritize equitable, integrated and high-quality health services based on digital technology and a 
highly trained workforce, and to encourage social participation, as the entities concerned 
understood the plight of the most vulnerable. Efforts must be made to work together on all areas 
to be addressed at the current Board session. His country was committed to the climate and 
health agenda, which it would focus on at the thirtieth session of the Conference of the Parties to 
the United Nations Climate Change Conference. 

The representative of CANADA welcomed the Secretariat’s work to strengthen 
organizational integrity, transparency and accountability, which it should pursue. It was essential 
to continue the reform process, as the success of the Organization’s work was predicated on the 
well-being of its workforce. Member States should return to first principles and guide the 
Organization, through action and intervention, as it implemented their priorities. It was imperative 
to provide the Secretariat with a single set of clear instructions since splitting focus across multiple 
resolutions led to a piecemeal approach, further straining resources and undermining the drive for 
efficiency gains. All resolutions were premised on the same fundamental approach and Member 
States should therefore provide guidance and signal priorities in a consolidated way through the 
core governance documents of the Fourteenth General Programme of Work, 2025–2028, and the 
Programme budget 2024–2025. 

The representative of CHINA, noting the significant gap between developed and developing

representation of developing countries and involve experts from those countries in its work. It 
should define performance indicators to assess the effectiveness of Member States’ contributions, 
and promote Member State-led decision-making to improve the health sector in developing 
countries and ensure achievement of the relevant Sustainable Development Goals. He stood ready

the WHO Academy in Lyon and urged all Member States to make use of it. His Government 
continued to defend the Organization, as the standard-setting body for public health, and 
multilateralism, as the means of ensuring an equitable international system that left no one 
behind. 

The representative of DENMARK3 said that WHO’s difficult financial situation would require 
tough strategic choices. The growing number of human-made emergencies and their impact on 
human health, such as in Ukraine and the Gaza Strip, were deeply deplorable. Conflict resulted not 
only in victims but also in the destruction of health infrastructure. Multilateral cooperation and 
innovation were important to secure the sustainability of health systems. 

 

3 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


Executive Board, 156th session  10 

 

The representative of the UNITED KINGDOM OF GREAT BRITAIN AND NORTHERN IRELAND4 
said that his Government had pledged millions of pounds in fully flexible funding in the 2024 
investment round to support the delivery of WHO’s transformation efforts. Commending WHO’s 
interventions in conflicts and crises, he said that 2025 would be a critical year for protecting global 
health. His Government remained committed to, inter alia, improving global health outcomes, 
protecting global health security, including through a new pandemic agreement, and tackling the 
health impacts of conflicts and noncommunicable diseases. International collaboration was crucial 
to achieving the collective goal of health for all, and his Government was keen to pursue its 
collaboration with WHO and Member States, including on prioritization efforts in the light of WHO 
budget pressures. 

The representative of MOZAMBIQUE,4 expressing deep thanks for WHO’s support in the face 
of disease outbreaks and climate disasters, observed that the Organization provided aid where 
others could not, its employees often working at great risk to their own safety and security. All 
Member States should make efforts to improve their contributions and mobilize more partners, to 
allow WHO to accomplish its purpose to promote health and prevent disease, particularly given 
the current financial crisis. Her Government was endeavouring to increase its assessed 
contribution and would try to contribute to the investment round. It was committed to working 
with other Member States to conclude the pandemic agreement in May 2025. 

The representative of ESWATINI4 reaffirmed his Government’s dedication to strengthening 
primary healthcare as the foundation for resilient health systems, ensuring services reached the 
most vulnerable; enhancing pandemic preparedness and response through regional collaboration 
and investment in health security; and addressing the double burden of disease. Decisions 
resulting from the discussions in the current Board session must translate into tangible 
improvements for all people, with global health equity at the centre of collective efforts. 

The representative of FINLAND4 said that, as things currently stood, the potential to reach 
the health-related Sustainable Development Goals by 2030 seemed to be slipping away. The 
Secretariat must guide Member States, provide accurate and up-to-date information and support 
responses to health threats. WHO and multilateral cooperation were key to ensuring sustainable 
and timely access to innovation and new technologies to address health challenges. Many 
Member States were limited in their ability to increase their assessed contributions and the 
withdrawal of WHO’s biggest financial contributor left a gaping hole in finances. WHO was also 
losing many of its critical experts, and its cost structure and activities must be adjusted. Solidarity 
and a pragmatic approach to prioritization were essential to ensuring that WHO’s crucial work 
continued. 

The representative of URUGUAY,4 describing measures taken in his country to address, inter 
alia, the impact of climate change on health and regulation of traditional healthcare, expressed 
gratitude to the Organization for tackling priority issues that affected global health and reaffirmed 
his commitment to the principles of the Organization. 

The representative of JAPAN4 said that WHO must fully leverage its expertise and take the 
lead, based on scientific evidence, to address global health challenges. It should prioritize 
infectious disease crisis management, as recent outbreaks had underscored the critical importance 
of disease prevention, preparedness and response. It should also prioritize its unique normative 
role, particularly in relation to the International Health Regulations (2005). 

 

4 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


Summary records: First meeting  11 

 

The representative of BANGLADESH5 said that international organizations were created 
precisely to provide international support when there were resource constraints at the national 
level. In view of the lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic, his Government strongly 
advocated diversification of production facilities across continents to make treatment available to 
all people. He expressed deep concern at the attacks on health services in conflict-stricken areas 
and urged that enhanced support be provided to the people of the Gaza Strip and Palestine. 
Despite the current financial constraints, interruptions to the WHO programme in vulnerable 
societies would be unfortunate and it fell to the Organization as a whole to sustain its activities. 
Caution should be exercised when addressing WHO expenditure on staff, taking into account that 
future recruits might be discouraged by career uncertainty. 

The representative of EL SALVADOR5 welcomed the report of the Director-General and 
outlined the progress made in his country with regard to measures to address the impact of 
climate change on health, among others. He supported efforts on digital training and artificial 
intelligence to optimize health services. Noting the budget challenges facing WHO, he trusted that 
the Organization would draw on its expertise to deliver results in an equitable and efficient 
manner. 

The representative of BOTSWANA5 said that, like many low- and middle-income countries, 
his country faced a disproportionately high burden of noncommunicable diseases. She therefore 
called on WHO to prioritize support for Member States to meet their noncommunicable disease 
targets ahead of the high-level meeting of the General Assembly on the prevention and control of 
non-communicable diseases in 2025. She remained optimistic that the Intergovernmental 
Negotiating Body would complete its work on the pandemic agreement in time for it to be 
considered at the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly. 

The representative of GERMANY5 called on all Member States to provide robust and 
sustainable financial support so that WHO could fulfil its mandate while maintaining its 
independence and responding to health emergencies. Financing WHO was a shared responsibility 
and an investment in both global health and national health systems. The current financial 
outlook, coupled with increasing demands from Member States, was concerning. Continuity of 
WHO’s essential programmes must be prioritized and the cost implications of new actions, 
including resolutions, must be assessed. She suggested that there be fewer resolutions and clear 
costing estimates from the outset. 

The representative of IRELAND,5 noting the intended withdrawal of the United States of 
America from WHO, expressed firm support for the Organization. In the face of global health 
challenges whose impact was felt collectively, beyond national borders, the international 
community had to work together. WHO’s growing responsibilities made financial sustainability and 
predictability crucial, and the cost implications of any new activities should therefore be assessed 
to ensure the continuity of existing essential programmes. 

The representative of CHAD5 welcomed the activities of the Organization, including the 
establishment of the WHO Academy, which would help to strengthen the capacities of workers on 
the ground. Outlining the situation in his country, particularly migratory flows of refugees and 
displaced persons, he called on international partners to support efforts to address the related 
challenges. Interruptions to the financing of the Organization would have a significant impact on 
people’s health in the African Region. 

 

5 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


Executive Board, 156th session  12 

 

The representative of the RUSSIAN FEDERATION6 said that the international community 
supported WHO in maintaining its leading role in global health and an effective selection process 
for the Organization’s priorities was therefore important. His Government was willing to continue 
to provide expertise and support to the Organization, particularly in fighting communicable and 
noncommunicable diseases. The inclusion on the agenda of irrelevant or politicized items had led 
to more important issues being ignored. Climate change issues were addressed under several 
agenda items, while other topics were addressed together, which made discussion more difficult. 
Restrictive measures taken by individual countries affected not only WHO but also ordinary people 
and prevented the sustainable financing of the Organization, thereby undermining its ability to 
respond to health emergencies. Decisions on, for example, the adoption of the pandemic 
agreement should be taken by consensus.  

The representative of NAMIBIA6 said that the theme of the 2025 World Health Day (Healthy 
beginnings, hopeful futures) was timely considering the approaching deadline for meeting the 
Sustainable Development Goals. The draft Proposed programme budget 2026–2027 and efforts to 
ensure transparency, efficiency and accountability in its formulation were welcome. He supported 
the 20% increase in assessed contributions and called for budget considerations that addressed 
country-specific priorities. Predictable, flexible and sustainable financing for WHO was essential, 
and the Organization’s resource mobilization efforts were therefore welcome. Investment in 
workforce training was crucial for strong and resilient health systems. 

The representative of BELGIUM6 condemned all attacks on healthcare professionals and 
infrastructure. The humanitarian situation in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo was 
alarming, and he called for respect for international humanitarian law and human rights. The 
intention of the United States of America to withdraw from the Organization was deeply 
regrettable, as it weakened multilateralism and global health. It was important to focus on the 
Organization’s core mission and to collectively foster meaningful multilateralism that delivered 
concrete results on the ground. WHO’s efforts to combat misinformation were also critical. He 
expressed concern about the inclusion on the Board’s agenda of numerous items that would entail 
sensitive and lengthy discussions, and would welcome a more streamlined decision-making 
process, with fewer resolutions, to obtain a realistic set of priorities. 

The meeting rose at 12:30. 

 

6 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


13 

 

 

 

Second meeting 

Monday, 3 February 2025, at 14:35 

Chair: Dr J.X. Walcott (Barbados) 

1. Report by the Director-General: Item 2 of the agenda (document EB156/2) (continued) 

The representative of SLOVAKIA said that the challenges ahead required decisive action, 
strategic prioritization and sustainable commitment from all Member States. To address 
challenges and sustain critical programmes, there was a need for innovative approaches, close 
collaboration with Member States through transparent priority reassessment; enhanced financial 
sustainability through flexible and innovative funding; and a more robust governance framework 
based on a science-led analysis of gaps and risks to ensure that new commitments aligned with 
available resources. Efforts to strengthen regulatory oversight should be accelerated to ensure 
equitable access to medicine and health technologies, particularly for vulnerable populations and 
those in humanitarian need. Sustainable financing models were needed to prevent catastrophic 
out-of-pocket spending. To tackle noncommunicable diseases, there should be greater technical 
and financial investment in WHO’s leadership role in the development of behavioural and social 
science to continue shaping effective public health innovations. The Organization’s financial 
realities must be addressed with reforms, efficiency and stronger global cooperation. He called on 
Member States to support WHO’s financial sustainability measures, including the proposed 
20% increase in assessed contributions; to engage constructively in governance reform, ensuring 
that WHO could remain focused on its most important and pressing priorities and normative role; 
and to strengthen global solidarity and multilateralism, recognizing that a well-funded and 
effective WHO was in the collective interest of all nations.  

The representative of TOGO expressed appreciation for the Secretariat’s continued support 
for Member States in combating communicable and noncommunicable diseases and in responding 
to health emergencies. She encouraged the broadening of the donor base and the optimal use of 
mobilized resources while prioritizing country needs. The Secretariat should also ensure flexibility, 
transparency and predictability in financing and in strengthening solidarity. 

The representative of GUINEA-BISSAU,1 commending the Organization for its stewardship 
and its contribution in the response to global health challenges, said that continued investment in 
public health was essential to prevent future crises and save lives.  

The representative of the PHILIPPINES1 said that WHO’s resilience would enable it to face 
sustainable financing challenges. By working closely with Member States and in line with the 
Fourteenth General Programme of Work, 2025–2028, WHO could fulfil its obligations in terms of 
global health governance. Carrying out the Organization’s mandate required consistent and 

 

1 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


Executive Board, 156th session 14 

 

sustainable financing. Member States must take bold and decisive action to ensure greater 
investment in health through increased assessed and voluntary contributions, in order to achieve 
the outputs and priorities set forth in the Fourteenth General Programme of Work, 2025–2028. 
His Government’s participation in the investment round had demonstrated that every economy 
could contribute substantially to sustaining regional and global efforts. He highlighted the 
importance of addressing shared health challenges through multilateralism and collective action. 
The priority should be to sustain, manage and adequately resource WHO, with a strong focus on 
results, value for money and equity. 

The representative of PORTUGAL2 said that urgent action was needed to integrate health 
into climate policies, ensuring mitigation and adaptation efforts to protect vulnerable populations. 
The fourth high-level meeting of the General Assembly on the prevention and control of non-
communicable diseases would provide a critical opportunity for strong commitments on 
prevention, early detection and equitable care to tackle the growing burden of noncommunicable 
diseases, including mental health.  

In view of the devastating effects of active conflicts on health systems and lives worldwide, 
he called for an end to hostilities and the protection of healthcare under international law. Global 
health challenges demanded solidarity, and the Organization’s role in uniting nations was 
indispensable. Member States must rally behind WHO to strengthen its mandate and safeguard 
global health.  

The representative of SINGAPORE2 said that, given budgetary concerns, there was greater 
impetus to advance the transformation agenda to make the Organization leaner and more 
effective. Member States should help WHO to prioritize its work to focus on the most impactful 
initiatives, informed by country and regional contexts. WHO must be adequately resourced to do 
its work; she therefore expressed support for the proposed 20% increase in assessed 
contributions.  

The Observer of PALESTINE said that while the occupied Palestinian territory, including east 
Jerusalem, had long been overrun by multiple emergencies, the year 2024 had been the worst yet, 
as Israeli attacks on healthcare facilities and workers had led to poliovirus outbreaks and the 
collapse of the public health system. Strong commitment was required from the international 
community to rebuild the Palestinian public health sector and support mental health programmes 
to address the trauma faced by Palestinians. WHO programmes must be sustainably funded.  

The representative of the PLURINATIONAL STATE OF BOLIVIA2 said that, amid global crises 
and actions that were challenging international law and undermining multilateralism, it was 
essential to promote dialogue and close cooperation with a view to strengthening WHO’s work, 
ensuring its effective functioning and overcoming contemporary challenges. The right to health 
must be defended through joint efforts, including on health systems strengthening and health 
emergency prevention, preparedness and response. An ambitious pandemic agreement was 
needed that centred on equity and solidarity, to enable a more effective pandemic response. She 
stressed the importance of avoiding politicization and double standards in WHO programmes and 
plans, which should adopt a gender-sensitive approach and include Indigenous Peoples and people 
in vulnerable situations; in particular, the draft global traditional medicine strategy: 2025–2034 
should ensure respect for and the preservation of Indigenous knowledge. 

 

2 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


Summary records: Second meeting 15 

 

The representative of SOUTH AFRICA3 expressed support for the continued predictable 
funding of WHO. Noting that the programme budgets for the implementation of the Fourteenth 
General Programme of Work, 2025–2028 were being drawn up during a time of financial and 
political difficulties, she called on the global community to remain resolute and foster innovation 
in responding to those challenges. Her Government continued to support the increase in assessed 
contributions, which should be coupled with robust resource mobilization efforts in the context of 
the investment round. Solidarity and commitment were needed from all actors if the world was to 
get back on track towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. In particular, a 
commitment to building resilient health systems by strengthening primary healthcare and 
ensuring universal health coverage would remain fundamental to the achievement of health 
equity. Addressing universal health coverage would be key to ensuring the availability of adequate 
human resources and implementing the Fourteenth General Programme of Work, 2025–2028. To 
support Member States in building relevant capacities, there was an urgent need to finalize the 
work of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body to draft and negotiate a WHO convention, 
agreement or other international instrument on pandemic prevention, preparedness and 
response. 

The representative of the ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN3 said that, at a time when 
multilateralism was under severe pressure, Member States needed to strengthen international 
solidarity and promote equity at the global level. Working together to bridge the gap between 
developing and developed countries would help to achieve the highest attainable standard of 
health for all. In the light of recent budgetary concerns, a realistic and comprehensive approach to 
adjusting or resetting the Organization’s priorities would support efforts to achieve its goals. The 
consultation process should remain inclusive and involve all Member States, including those in the 
Eastern Mediterranean Region, which were the most affected by debilitating challenges.  

The representative of the UNITED REPUBLIC OF TANZANIA3 urged Member States to finalize 
negotiations on a pandemic agreement through the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body. 
Collective efforts among Member States and partners were needed to address persistent 
challenges such as limited access to healthcare, inadequate health infrastructure and the need for 
robust health data systems. 

The representative of MALAYSIA3 expressed support for the Fourteenth General Programme 
of Work, 2025–2028. The base segment of the programme budget should respond to the unique 
needs of Member States and seek to strengthen country capacities and enhance WHO’s 
accountability. Her Government remained committed to the proposed 20% increase in assessed 
contributions, which should be accompanied by appropriate governance reforms and 
improvements in transparency, efficiency, accountability and compliance. Member States should 
support the investment round to increase voluntary contributions.  

There was an urgent need to address health challenges such as the increasing burden of 
noncommunicable diseases, communicable diseases and climate change. Hospitals and health 
facilities must remain safe havens for patients and health workers. Her Government continued to 
advocate for the rights of the Palestinian people and would play a role in rebuilding the Gaza Strip. 
She invited countries to mobilize efforts to rebuild the Gaza Strip and the occupied Palestinian 
territory and to alleviate the suffering of the Palestinian population.  

The representative of ZAMBIA3 underscored the importance of realistic and pragmatic 
budgeting, and priority-setting criteria in budget allocation that focused on WHO’s core functions 

 

3 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board. 


Executive Board, 156th session 16 

 

and country-level interventions. The Secretariat should prepare a comprehensive analysis 
regarding priority-setting and the impact of additional activities on the programme budget. In the 
light of the significant budgetary implications of recent resolutions on the draft Proposed 
programme budget 2026–2027, she expressed support for a further review and streamlining of 
resolutions and decisions. It was necessary to find innovative ways to broaden the donor base to 
reduce dependency on earmarked funds. 

The DIRECTOR-GENERAL thanked Member States for expressing their confidence in the 
multilateral system and highlighting the central role played by WHO in global health. The 
Secretariat would work hard to ensure that the Organization continued to adapt to changing 
situations. Member States’ support for sustainable financing was deeply appreciated since 
volatility and a lack of flexibility in funding made it difficult to plan and provide tailored support to 
countries, thus hindering the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Sustainable 
financing would also help the Secretariat to support staff employed on temporary rolling 
contracts. He encouraged Member States to support the second phase of the proposed increase in 
assessed contributions, which would be especially important in view of the current situation. The 
Secretariat would welcome further guidance from Member States with regard to new financing 
mechanisms. 

The Board noted the report. 

2. Report of the regional committees to the Executive Board: Item 3 of the agenda 
(document EB156/3) 

The representative of QATAR, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region, said that discussions at the 71st session of the WHO Regional Committee 
for the Eastern Mediterranean had underscored a shared commitment to strengthening health 
systems, improving access to essential health services and addressing pressing health challenges 
that had a disproportionate impact on the Region. Member States had recognized that achieving 
universal health coverage and sustainable development required collective action, political will 
and strategic investment in public health. The endorsement of the Strategic Operational Plan for 
the Eastern Mediterranean Region, 2025–2028, had demonstrated the Region’s ambition to build 
more resilient, responsive and equitable health systems. That vision would be translated into 
action aimed at tackling public health challenges such as improving trauma care in humanitarian 
settings, combating antimicrobial resistance and promoting mental health support in emergencies. 
Strengthening local vaccine production capacities, laboratory services and the digital 
transformation of the health system would be crucial to the provision of timely and quality 
healthcare services. Member States in the Region remained committed to accelerating progress 
on the Immunization Agenda 2030. 

Effective governance and sustainable financing were essential to translating strategies into 
actions. Discussions on WHO’s investment case, the programme budget and ongoing global health 
negotiations had reinforced the importance of securing predictable resources and ensuring that 
WHO remained fit for purpose in responding to global and regional health challenges. Member 
States had reaffirmed their commitment to addressing noncommunicable diseases, including by 
extending the mandate of the High-level Ministerial Group on the Control of Tobacco and 
Emerging Tobacco and Nicotine Products in the Eastern Mediterranean Region and calling for 
stronger regional and global collaboration to tackle other public health threats.  


Summary records: Second meeting 17 

 

The representative of ZIMBABWE, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the African 
Region, offered condolences for the passing of the Regional Director-elect, Dr Faustine Ndugulile. 
Issues of particular importance for his Region included the rising burden of noncommunicable 
diseases, owing to ageing populations, urbanization, globalization and trade and limited 
healthcare infrastructure; the slow progress of negotiations on the pandemic agreement, 
especially considering recent infectious disease outbreaks in the Region; and the need to build 
sustainable health systems. Climate-resilient programmes must be scaled up in the Region, given 
the need to protect livelihoods, enhance food security, support human health, reduce poverty and 
inequality and promote sustainable development. 

The Member States of the Region had been fully involved in the Organization’s initial 
investment round, which would create an Organization capable of taking the lead on pressing 
global health threats and initiatives. Establishing a fund similar to the South-East Asia Regional 
Health Emergency Fund could help countries in the African Region to mount a swift response to 
natural disasters, epidemics and other crises, improve coordination and collaboration, enhance 
preparedness and resilience and increase accountability and transparency. Increasing multilateral 
collaboration to support local manufacture of medicines, vaccines and other technologies would 
improve access to vaccines, create jobs, boost health security and reduce dependence on 
external aid. 

The representative of the REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA commended the efforts made by the 
Secretariat and the regional committees in fostering alignment between regional and global health 
priorities and welcomed decisions adopted by the WHO Regional Committee for Europe on 
preparedness, response and resilience; resilient and sustainable health systems; and emergency 
medical teams. Equitable access to medical products, local vaccine production and health 
workforce resilience were essential to achieving universal health coverage and sustainable 
healthcare financing. 

The representative of TOGO commended the WHO Regional Office for Africa on the 
implementation of the transformation agenda and flagship health emergency prevention, 
preparedness and response initiatives. She called on the Secretariat to support the realization of 
an expedited process for the nomination of a new Regional Director for Africa; ensure equitable 
resource allocation, taking into account regional priorities; expedite negotiations on a pandemic 
agreement; and strengthen multisectoral collaboration. 

The representative of INDONESIA4 noted with appreciation the discussions on the 
reassignment of her country from the South-East Asia Region to the Western Pacific Region, which 
had taken place at recent meetings of the regional committees

Resolutions 

WHA78.1 WHO Pandemic Agreement1 

The Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, 

Recalling decisions SSA2(5) (2021) and WHA77(20) (2024), which, acknowledging the need to 
address gaps in preventing, preparing for and responding to health emergencies, inter alia, 
established the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body to draft and negotiate a WHO convention, 
agreement or other international instrument on pandemic prevention, preparedness and 
response (the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body), with a view to adoption under Article 19, or 
under other provisions of the WHO Constitution; 

Expressing appreciation for the work of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body, including 
its outcome as contained in document A78/10, and acknowledging with appreciation the 
leadership of its Bureau; 

Reaffirming the need for a legally binding international instrument on pandemic prevention, 
preparedness and response, in line with decisions SSA2(5) and WHA77(20); 

Emphasizing the role of the International Health Regulations (2005), adopted through 
resolution WHA58.3 (2005), and subsequently amended through resolutions WHA67.13 (2014), 
WHA75.12 (2022), and WHA77.17 (2024), in pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, 
and the need for coherence and complementarity in the implementation of the International 
Health Regulations (2005) and the WHO Pandemic Agreement; 

Recognizing the continuing threat of pathogens with pandemic potential which calls for 
enhancing pandemic prevention, preparedness and response and for refraining from taking 
measures that adversely affect it, 

1. ADOPTS, pursuant to Article 19 of the Constitution of the World Health Organization, the 
WHO Pandemic Agreement as shown in Annex 1 to the present document; 

2. RECOGNIZES that the adoption of the WHO Pandemic Agreement by the Health Assembly 
does not prejudice the sovereign prerogative of each State to consider the WHO Pandemic 
Agreement in accordance with its constitutional processes; 

3. NOTES, in accordance with Article 31 of the WHO Pandemic Agreement, that the WHO 
Pandemic Agreement shall be open for signature after adoption of the Annex described in  
Article 12 of the Agreement by the Health Assembly, at the World Health Organization 
headquarters in Geneva, and thereafter at United Nations Headquarters in New York, on dates to 
be determined by the World Health Assembly; 

 

1 See Annex 5 for the financial and administrative implications for the Secretariat of this resolution. 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly 4 

 

4. CALLS UPON all States and regional economic integration organizations entitled to do so, to 
consider signing, ratifying, accepting, approving, formally confirming or acceding to the WHO 
Pandemic Agreement at the earliest opportunity in line with Articles 31 and 32 of the Agreement, 
with a view to bringing the WHO Pandemic Agreement, including its Annex described in Article 12, 
into force as soon as possible; 

5. URGES all States and regional economic integration organizations to take all appropriate 
measures, pending the entry into force of the WHO Pandemic Agreement, to further its objective 
and eventual implementation, guided by equity and the principle of solidarity with all people and 
countries in the context of health emergencies, to prevent, prepare for and respond to pandemic 
emergencies, and public health emergencies of international concern; 

6. URGES all States and regional economic integration organizations, in the event a pandemic 
emergency is determined prior to the entry into force of the WHO Pandemic Agreement, to take 
measures, promptly, on a voluntary basis, in line with relevant provisions of the WHO Pandemic 
Agreement, noting that taking such measures is without prejudice to the position of any State or 
regional economic integration organization with regard to the WHO Pandemic Agreement; 

7. URGES all Member States, regional economic integration organizations, observers and 
relevant stakeholders to support the preparatory activities referred to in this resolution and to 
effectively encourage prompt entry into force and implementation of the WHO Pandemic 
Agreement; 

8. CALLS UPON the United Nations and invites other relevant international organizations to 
continue to provide support for strengthening pandemic prevention, preparedness and response; 

9. DECIDES, in accordance with Rule 41 of its Rules of Procedure, to establish an open-ended 
Intergovernmental Working Group (IGWG) to: 

(1) as a priority, draft and negotiate the Annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement 
described in Article 12 of the WHO Pandemic Agreement and submit the outcome to the 
Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly for its consideration, and subsequently facilitate, as 
necessary, activities related to the adoption of said Annex and the opening for signature, 
ratification, acceptance, approval, accession or formal confirmation of the WHO Pandemic 
Agreement; 

(2) following completion of the activities in paragraph (1) above, conduct preparatory 
work on the following issues in the WHO Pandemic Agreement for consideration, as 
appropriate, by the Conference of the Parties: 

(a) rules of procedure for the Conference of the Parties, and its criteria for 
participation of observers at its proceedings; 

(b) financial rules for the Conference of the Parties and any subsidiary bodies it may 
establish; 

(c) a draft budget for the first financial period; 

(d) the structure, functions and modalities of the Global Supply Chain and Logistics 
Network as referred to in Article 13 of the WHO Pandemic Agreement; 


Resolutions and decisions 5 

 

(e) the information, frequency and format of the reports required under Article 21.1 
on the implementation of the WHO Pandemic Agreement, including Article 11.1(a); 

(f) the mechanism referred to in WHO Pandemic Agreement Article 19.5 and 19.6 to

WHA78.3 Strengthening the evidence base for public health and social 
measures12 

The Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, 

Having considered the report by the Director-General;13 

Noting that public health and social measures refer to nonpharmaceutical measures 
implemented by individuals, communities, governments and institutions to reduce the risk and 
scale of epidemic- and pandemic-prone infectious disease transmission; 

Acknowledging the relevance of public health and social measures to the International 
Health Regulations (2005), the amendments to which were adopted through resolution 
WHA77.17 (2024); 

Recalling the temporary recommendations of the International Health Regulations (2005) 
Emergency Committee regarding the pandemic of coronavirus disease (COVID-19), issued by the 
Director-General to States Parties on, inter alia, the continued use of evidence-informed and  
risk-based public health and social measures; and recalling the temporary recommendations of 
the International Health Regulations (2005) Emergency Committee regarding the upsurge of mpox 
2024 to States Parties on addressing research gaps and generating evidence, including in respect 
of the effectiveness of public health interventions; 

Recalling also resolution WHA58.5 (2005) on strengthening pandemic-influenza 
preparedness and response, which urged Member States to make effective use of appropriate and 
effective public health and social measures to protect the general public from the influenza virus; 

Acknowledging the importance of public health and social measures in preventing and 
controlling infectious diseases, especially those with epidemic and pandemic potential; and 
acknowledging that public health and social measures are the first, and sometimes the only, 
interventions available, and that appropriate public health and social measures are essential 
throughout an epidemic or pandemic; 

Noting that it can be difficult to anticipate who may be most at risk of experiencing adverse 
health and socioeconomic consequences during future epidemics and pandemics, as well as 
possible adverse effects of public health and social measures; and that building a stronger and

robust evidence base for public health and social measures can help to improve understanding 
and better inform approaches to minimize such adverse consequences; 

Recognizing that, despite the critical role of public health and social measures in preventing

effectiveness and impact of public health and social measures are limited; 

Acknowledging the importance of expanding the evidence base to inform the 
implementation of public health and social measures that are targeted, effective, appropriate,

specific risks and hazards, and that aim to maximize public health benefits, while minimizing their

Acknowledging also the importance of increasing understanding of the drivers and barriers, 
including behavioural factors, that prevent or enable national implementation and community and

Recognizing the inherent challenges in conducting research on public health and social 
measures owing to their complex, multisectoral nature, and that national research, ethical and

Recalling resolution WHA58.34 (2005) on the Ministerial Summit on Health Research, in 
which the Health Assembly acknowledged that high-quality, ethical research and the generation 
and application of knowledge are critical for achieving internationally agreed health-related 
development goals, and resolution WHA63.21 (2010), which outlined WHO’s role and

emergency and preparedness policies; 

Recognizing that research on public health and social measures should be well designed, 
methodologically rigorous and well implemented, in accordance with applicable ethical guidelines

Expressing grave concern at the catastrophic humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip, and its 
vast consequences for the civilian population, and in light of the gravity of the current escalating 
situation, and the magnitude of the intense damage on the public health sector, that has, to this
