WHA78.5 Promoting and prioritizing an integrated lung health approach22 

The Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, 

Having considered the consolidated report by the Director-General;23 

Noting with deep concern that, in 2021, communicable and noncommunicable lung diseases, 
including coronavirus disease (COVID-19), were among the leading causes of mortality, causing 
more than 18 million deaths globally; 

Recognizing the critical importance of addressing both communicable and 
noncommunicable diseases that affect the lungs, including tuberculosis, pneumonia, influenza, 
COVID-19, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary fibrosis, asthma and lung cancer, 
and the need to strengthen primary healthcare in the context of an integrated approach towards 
attainment of universal health coverage; and acknowledging that pulmonary diseases and other 
noncommunicable diseases often share the same risk factors, requiring a horizontal preventive 
approach; 

Stressing the importance of comprehensive infection prevention and control measures to 
reduce the risk of transmission of tuberculosis, COVID-19, pneumonia and other airborne 
infectious diseases, particularly in high-burden, low-income settings; and recognizing the critical 
role of addressing risk factors and determinants, including poor and crowded living conditions, 
poor ventilation and others; 

Acknowledging indoor and outdoor air pollution, whose root cause is predominantly 
socioeconomic in nature,24 and its linkage with social and environmental determinants of health as 
one of the leading risk factors for lung diseases,25 especially in developing countries that are 
disproportionately impacted, as well as the need for multisectoral engagement and action to 
promote lung health, prevent new cases of disease and reduce exacerbations of respiratory 
conditions; 

 

22 See Annex 5 for the financial and administrative implications for the Secretariat of this resolution. 

23 Document A78/4. 

24 See resolution WHA68.8 (2015). 

25 WHO ambient air quality database, 2022 update: status report. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023 
(accessed 26 February 2025). 

https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240047693


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly 18 

 

Recognizing that radon exposure is one of the leading causes of lung cancer after smoking in 
countries with known data, and acknowledging the lack of prevention and mitigating actions for 
radon exposure, as well as limited public awareness concerning radon risks; 

Re-emphasizing that over 45% of tobacco-related deaths are due to lung diseases, totalling 
3.3 million deaths in 2021,26 and acknowledging that exposure to second-hand smoke causes 
cancer and that vaping aerosols can be harmful to lung health, which underscores the importance 
of primary care services for prevention of tobacco smoking, particularly tobacco and vaping 
control; 

Noting the substantial contribution of workplace exposures to the burden of both infectious 
and chronic respiratory diseases; 

Acknowledging the impact of stigma associated with lung cancer, tuberculosis and chronic 
obstructive pulmonary disease on access to early detection and access to treatment, noting 
advances in lung screening and its effectiveness in reducing mortality rates in high-risk 
populations; 

Recalling United Nations General Assembly resolution 74/2 (2019) and its commitment to 
strengthen efforts to address noncommunicable diseases as part of universal health coverage, the 
political declaration of the high-level meeting of the General Assembly on the prevention and 
control of non-communicable diseases,27 the political declaration of the third high-level meeting of 
the General Assembly on the prevention and control of non-communicable diseases of 2018,28 
which reaffirms the primary role and responsibility of governments in responding to the challenge 
of noncommunicable diseases by developing adequate national multisectoral and participative 
responses for their prevention and control, and the Rio Political Declaration on Social 
Determinants of Health (2011), considering that health inequalities are an important aspect for 
respiratory diseases; 

Recognizing resolution WHA72.2 (2019) on primary health care, in which the Health 
Assembly urged Member States to implement the commitments of the Declaration of Astana, 
resolution WHA60.26 (2007) on workers’ health: global plan of action, through which Member 
States were urged to work towards full coverage of all workers with essential interventions and 
basic occupational health services for primary prevention of occupational and work-related 
diseases and injuries, and the significant progress in implementing WHO’s global action plan for 
the prevention and control of noncommunicable diseases 2013–2020, endorsed by the Health 
Assembly in resolution WHA66.10 (2013), including the 2022 update of Appendix 3 to that global 
action plan, endorsed by the Health Assembly in decision WHA76(9) (2023), and the adoption of 
the related implementation roadmap 2023–2030 through decision WHA75(11) (2022), as well as 
the WHO global strategy on health, environment and climate change, noted through decision 
WHA72(9) (2019), resolution WHA68.8 (2015) on health and the environment: addressing the 
health impact of air pollution, and its roadmap, welcomed by the Health Assembly in decision 
WHA69(11) (2016), and resolution WHA70.12 (2017) on cancer prevention and control in the 
context of an integrated approach; 

 

26 Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation. Global Burden of Disease study, 2021 data (accessed 
26 February 2025). 

27 United Nations General Assembly resolution 66/2 (2011). 

28 United Nations General Assembly resolution 73/2 (2018). 

https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/
https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/


Resolutions and decisions 19 

 

Recalling resolution WHA71.3 (2018) on preparation for a high-level meeting of the General 
Assembly on ending tuberculosis, which reaffirmed commitment to end the tuberculosis epidemic 
by 2030, and the resulting political declaration of the high-level meeting on the fight against 
tuberculosis (2023),29 as well as resolution WHA67.1 (2014) on the global strategy and targets for 
tuberculosis prevention, care and control after 2015, which set ambitious targets for reducing 
tuberculosis incidence and mortality; and emphasizing the importance of the WHO multisectoral 
accountability framework for tuberculosis to enable universal access to good-quality services, and 
to address all determinants and drivers of tuberculosis, such as poverty, inequalities, 
undernutrition, HIV infection, noncommunicable diseases and inadequate housing and living 
conditions, as an integral part of the universal health coverage agenda, including in the context of 
health and humanitarian emergencies; 

Recalling also resolution WHA76.5 (2023) on strengthening diagnostics capacity, resolution 
WHA72.8 (2019) on improving the transparency of markets for medicines, vaccines, and other 
health products, the global strategy and plan of action on public health, innovation and intellectual 
property, adopted by the Health Assembly through resolution WHA61.21 (2008) and resolution 
WHA67.22 (2014) on access to essential medicines;  

Reaffirming resolution WHA73.1 (2020) on the COVID-19 response, which emphasized the 
need for equitable access to quality, safe, efficacious, effective and affordable diagnostics, 
therapeutics, medicines and vaccines for the COVID-19 response consistent with the provisions of 
relevant international treaties, including the provisions of the Agreement on Trade-Related 
Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS Agreement) and the flexibilities within the Doha 
Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and Public Health; 

Noting resolution WHA72.6 (2019) on global action on patient safety, which is crucial in the 
management of both communicable and noncommunicable lung diseases; 

Recalling the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and reaffirming the principles 
of primary healthcare as the basis for strengthening health systems;  

Building on the successes of the integrated approaches to disease management, including 
WHO’s existing instruments such as the Practical Approach to Lung Health, the WHO package of 
essential noncommunicable disease interventions for primary health care and Integrated 
Management of Childhood Illness in improving health outcomes, and their potential for integrated 
lung health programmes, 

1. URGES Member States,30 considering national context and priorities, and in alignment with 
relevant policies on addressing communicable, noncommunicable and occupational lung diseases: 

(1) to develop integrated national policy for an integrated approach to lung health, 
encompassing both communicable and noncommunicable lung diseases, through 
multisectoral collaboration and multidisciplinary collaboration and by incorporating  
whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches, ensuring engagement from all 
relevant sectors including health, environment, labour, education and finance; 

 

29 United Nations General Assembly resolution 78/5 (2023). 

30 And, where applicable, regional economic integration organizations. 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly 20 

 

(2) to incorporate an integrated approach to lung health into primary healthcare services 
towards the attainment of universal health coverage, inclusive of comprehensive lung health 
services, with effective referral pathways to secondary and tertiary care, when appropriate;  

(3) to strengthen awareness of the health impacts of air pollution and enhance national 
air quality standards and monitoring capacity; 

(4) to create and enforce adequate regulations protecting workers from occupational risk 
factors impacting lung health; 

(5) to strengthen existing, or establish new, comprehensive integrated approach lung 
health programmes including: 

(a) strengthening health promotion, primary preventive services – particularly 
tobacco and vaping control, reducing indoor and outdoor air pollution exposure – and 
vaccination programmes for preventable respiratory infections;  

(b) updating or developing evidence-based clinical and public health guidelines for 
cost-effective measures for early detection, diagnosis and treatment of communicable 
and noncommunicable lung diseases, including the use of innovative technologies;  

(c) updating or developing evidence-based information mechanisms for 
policy-making and programme monitoring, evaluation and learning;  

(6) to strengthen national capacities for an integrated approach on lung health, 
considering adaptation of relevant existing and evidence-based WHO tools to create an 
evidence-based and cost-effective integrated lung health package of interventions suitable 
for all patients, according to their individual needs; 

(7) to improve access to and affordability and availability of safe, effective and quality 
medicines, vaccines and health technologies using the WHO Model List of Essential 
Medicines and the WHO Model List of Essential In Vitro Diagnostics with an emphasis on 
cost-effectiveness, sustainable allocation of resources and evidence-based approaches 
including by increasing national capacities, and with a focus on building effective regulatory 
systems, manufacturing capacities and/or procurement strategies and policies for fair pricing 
to address both communicable and noncommunicable lung diseases, including tuberculosis, 
pneumonia, influenza and COVID-19, as well as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 
asthma, pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer; 

2. REQUESTS the Director-General: 

(1) to map existing strategies, road maps and WHO’s normative work and instruments 
relating to relevant lung conditions and risk factors, thereby helping to inform an integrated 
lung health approach and identify existing gaps and needs in addressing prevention, 
diagnosis and treatment of and rehabilitation from communicable and noncommunicable 
diseases; 


Resolutions and decisions 21 

 

(2) to provide an initial report with recommendations and key components to further 
strengthen an integrated lung health approach, to consider steps to improve 
implementation of existing strategies and plans in the context of an integrated lung health 
approach and to consider new initiatives, including a framework for tracking implementation 
of such strategies, plans and new proposals with clear measurable targets in consultation 
with Member States and other relevant stakeholders in line with the Framework of 
Engagement with Non-State Actors, as applicable, and to submit the report for consideration 
by the Eightieth World Health Assembly in 2027; 

(3) to collaborate with relevant stakeholders in line with the Framework of Engagement 
with Non-State Actors, as applicable, to mobilize commitment and resources, build capacity 
and foster collaborative research on the integrated lung health approach; 

(4) to provide support to Member States in strengthening their primary healthcare 
systems to effectively deliver integrated lung health services to strengthen universal health 
coverage, promoting a life-course approach to lung health; 

(5) to strengthen the capacity of the Secretariat to provide support for the 
implementation of cost-effective interventions and country-adapted models of care for both 
communicable and noncommunicable lung diseases, including tuberculosis, pneumonia, 
influenza and COVID-19, as well as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, 
pulmonary fibrosis and lung cancer; 

(6) to report on progress made in implementing this resolution to the Eightieth World 
Health Assembly in 2027 and the Eighty-first World Health Assembly in 2028. 

(Seventh plenary meeting, 27 May 2025 – 
Committee A, fourth report) 

WHA78.6 Reducing the burden of noncommunicable diseases through 
promotion of kidney health and strengthening prevention and 
control of kidney disease31 

The Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly, 

Having considered the consolidated report by the Director-General;32 

Recognizing the right of every human being, without distinction of any kind, to the 
enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health;  

Reaffirming our collective commitment to reducing premature mortality from 
noncommunicable diseases by one third, and achieving the targets in the WHO global action plan 
for the prevention and control of noncommunicable diseases 2013–2030,33 as committed to in the 
political declarations of the three high-level meetings of the General Assembly on the prevention 
and control of non-communicable diseases,34 including the nine voluntary global targets to 

 

31 See Annex 5 for the financial and administrative implications for the Secretariat of this resolution. 

32 Document A78/4. 

33 See resolution WHA66.10 (2013) and decision WHA72(11) (2019). 

34 See United Nations General Assembly resolutions 66/2 (2011), 68/300 (2014) and 73/2 (2018). 


Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly 22 

 

prevent and control noncommunicable diseases to be achieved by 2025, through effective health 
promotion and disease prevention, resilient health systems, an adequate, well-trained and 
committed health workforce, universal health coverage and people-centred health services, as 
well as the need to promote access and maintain essential services for noncommunicable diseases 
in emergencies and humanitarian settings;35 

Reaffirming also our commitment to accelerate the implementation of the 2019 and 2023 
political declarations of the high-level meetings of the General Assembly on universal health 
coverage, by providing financial risk protection, access to quality essential healthcare services and 
access to safe, effective, quality and cost-effective essential medicines and vaccines for all;36 

Recognizing that about 674 million people live with chronic kidney disease, comprising 9% of 
the global population, and concerned that kidney disease is one of the fastest-growing causes of 
death globally and is projected to become the fifth leading cause of death by 2050, with a 
projected 33% increase in age-standardized death rate and a 28% increase in age-standardized 
disability-adjusted life years if no action is taken; 

Recalling resolution WHA77.4 (2024) on increasing the availability, ethical access and 
oversight of transplantation of human cells, tissues and organs, in which the Health Assembly 
urges countries to adopt preventive strategies and incorporate transplantation into the continuum 
of care of noncommunicable and other diseases that may lead to the need for transplantation in 
accordance with their national contexts, and which requests the Director-General to provide 
support to Member States in implementing the elements of the resolution, particularly through 
the design of a global strategy on donation and transplantation;  

Concerned that access to kidney care is highly inequitable worldwide, especially in 
resource-limited settings, where kidney disease often goes undiagnosed and untreated, leaving 
millions at risk of death; 

Concerned also that in many developing countries, including small island developing States, 
individuals bear heavy financial burdens, needing to pay out of pocket for kidney care, as only a 
small percentage of these countries provide coverage for kidney replacement therapy (dialysis and 
transplantation), making kidney disease the leading cause of catastrophic health expenditure; 

Further concerned that kidney disease significantly impacts economies and societies, 
requires complex management and contributes disproportionately to national healthcare costs;  

Recognizing that kidney disease affects many individuals with common risk factors, is 
present in 1 in 5 people with hypertension and occurs in 4 of 10 people with diabetes, contributing 
to 1 in 10 deaths attributed to hypertension and accounting for a substantial proportion of 
morbidity and mortality related to diabetes; 

Aware that cost-effective medications for kidney disease are now available, continue to be 
developed and can dramatically reduce morbidity and mortality from kidney disease as well as 
other noncommunicable diseases that often coexist with kidney disease, such as hypertension, 
diabetes and cardiovascular disease, but concerned that these highly effective medicines, as well 

 

35 See United Nations General Assembly resolution 78/4 (2023). 

36 See United Nations General Assembly resolutions 74/2 (2019) and 78/4 (2023). 


Resolutions and decisions 23 

 

as diagnostics and consumables necessary for the spectrum of kidney care, are unaffordable or 
unavailable in many developing countries; 

Recognizing that kidney disease is a preventable but potentially fatal consequence of many 
infections in adults, adolescents and children, including malaria, dengue fever, HIV, tuberculosis, 
hepatitis, sepsis, coronavirus disease (COVID-19), diarrhoeal illnesses and neglected tropical 
diseases; 

Recognizing also that kidney disease is a significant risk factor for, and consequence of, 
hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (impacting 1 in 10 pregnancies) and that both kidney disease 
and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are associated with maternal mortality and preterm and 
low-birth-weight neonates, who are at higher risk of kidney disease; 

Further recognizing that kidney health is strongly impacted across the life course by all 
determinants37 of health, environmental factors and climate change, most disproportionately 
affecting developing countries and small island developing States;  

Also recognizing the urgent need to address, where appropriate, the social and 
environmental determinants of health, including climate change, to control the epidemic of 
chronic kidney disease of unknown origin which disproportionately affects young people in 
agricultural communities, and which places kidney disease among the top four causes of death in 
some regions; 

Recognizing further that the majority of people living with kidney disease have multiple 
comorbidities requiring specialized care across sectors to manage various health issues effectively, 
and that kidney disease significantly impacts mental health, causing stress, anxiety and 
depression, which further contribute to the decline in their health-related quality of life; 

Acknowledging that efforts have been made to strengthen services for treating 
noncommunicable diseases in emergencies,38 but recognizing that persons living with kidney 
disease remain highly vulnerable in humanitarian settings, especially those living on dialysis or 
with kidney transplants; 

Recognizing the importance of public awareness, health literacy, patient education and 
empowerment, community engagement, and policy action in controlling risk factors for and 
improving outcomes in individuals affected by kidney disease; 

Emphasizing the importance of integrating kidney health and the spectrum of kidney care 
into broader and holistic strategies for preventing and controlling noncommunicable diseases and 
recognizing the need for multisectoral approaches;39 

Considering that among the different types of kidney replacement therapies, kidney 
transplantation should be the preferred option for medically eligible patients with kidney failure, 
who should be systematically considered for this kind of treatment in accordance with their

4. OUTCOME OF THE SEVENTY-SEVENTH WORLD HEALTH ASSEMBLY: Item 3 of 
the agenda 
The CHAIR invited the Board to discuss the outcome of the Seventy-seventh World Health 
Assembly, noting that the follow-up to decision WHA77(15) (2024) on the process of handling and 
investigating potential allegations against WHO Directors-General would initially be discussed in a 
closed session, prior to the holding of discussion in a public session. 
The representative of BRAZIL welcomed the achievements of the Seventy-seventh World Health 
Assembly and highlighted the establishment of the single drafting group to consider matters related to 
the work of both the Working Group on Amendments to the International Health Regulations (2005) 
and the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body to draft and negotiate a WHO convention, agreement or 
other international instrument on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response.  
There was no room for polarization or politicization in health; health inclusivity and equity should 
be at the core of WHO’s work. Consensus-building was a key principle of WHO, and as such, the record 
number of votes at the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly was regrettable. Member States should 
work together to achieve health for all. Division among Member States would only fuel disinformation, 
misinformation and isolationism. He welcomed resolution WHA77.15 (2024) on aligning the 
participation of Palestine in the World Health Organization with its participation in the United Nations, 
which would increase WHO’s inclusivity and efficiency.  
He commended the Working Group on Amendments to the International Health 
Regulations (2005) for adding equity and solidarity to its governing principles and reaching agreement 
on access to health products and financing arrangements. That progress would also contribute to the 
work of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body, leading to a meaningful and ambitious pandemic 
agreement, with a focus on equity. He highlighted the importance of sustainable and predictable 
financing for the Organization as a whole. 
The representative of BRUNEI DARUSSALAM expressed the hope that a successful investment 
round would place the Fourteenth General Programme of Work, 2025–2028, on a path towards 
predictable and sustainable financing and would accelerate action on global health challenges and 
provide tailored support for Member States. He commended the adoption of resolution

He commended the significant progress made to strengthen the global health security architecture,

With regard to the staff mobility policy, measures should be put in place to ensure predictability 
for staff and protect WHO’s normative functions. The policy should also recognize current realities, in 
particular the challenge of dual-career households, while also providing effective relocation support and 
ensuring gender equity and safeguards for those in vulnerable categories. Staff posted at hardship duty

(5) to request the co-lead for Member State-led governance reform, with the support of 
Secretariat, to continue to provide regular informal progress reports to Member States 
regarding development of the revised draft, starting with initial briefings on the current 
document with all interested WHO regions to foster a shared understanding of the approach 
and considerations already taken in developing the procedures presented to  
Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly; 
(6) to request the Independent Expert Oversight Advisory Committee, and Secretariat 
staff that are appropriately positioned and capable of providing impartial guidance free of 
any real or perceived conflicts of interest in the outcome of the draft procedures,and 
Independent Expert Oversight Advisory Committee to provide timely advice and/or 
support to Member States.  
The CHAIR invited the Committee to proceed with the discussion of the amended draft decision 
proposed by the representative of the United States of America. 
The representative of AUSTRALIA said that the chapeau of the amended draft decision should 
reflect the wording used in paragraph 1 of the amended draft decision and should be amended to read: 
“Process for handling and investigating allegations against WHO Directors-General”. 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA said that her proposed amendments 
to paragraph 2 of the draft decision were intended to clarify that the Health Assembly had called for the 
leads for Member State governance reform to finalize the draft procedures rather than a draft process. 
The representative of SWITZERLAND, highlighting that regional coordinators were not formally 
recognized by WHO, proposed that, in amended paragraph 2, the words, “assisted by the regional 
coordinators” should be amended to read: “including by involving regional groups.” 
The representative of BULGARIA, expressing support for the proposal by the representative of 
Switzerland, said that, while the regional coordinators network was beneficial, it was not 
institutionalized.  
The representative of SLOVAKIA suggested that, in order to ensure unified language throughout 
the draft decision and in the light of the term “regional discussions” in amended paragraph 4, in amended 
60 EXECUTIVE BOARD, 155TH SESSION  
 
 
 
 
paragraph 2, the words, “consultations on this matter, assisted by the regional coordinators” should be 
amended to read: “consultations on this matter at the regional level”. 
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA proposed that, in paragraph 2, the 
words, “assisted by the regional coordinators” should be amended to read: “including by involving 
additional regional representatives”. 
The representative of SLOVAKIA expressed support for the proposal by the representative of the 
United States of America. 
The representative of ETHIOPIA suggested that, in amended paragraph 2, the words, 
“consultations on this matter, assisted by the regional coordinators” should be replaced with the words, 
“consultations at the regional level”. While the phrase “at the regional level” referred to the WHO 
regions, which might differ from the draft decision’s intended meaning, it was broader than “regional 
representatives” and would ensure more clarity for Member States, thus limiting the risk of reopening 
discussions on the draft decision at the next Health Assembly.  
The representative of SLOVENIA1 said that his Government was currently serving as a regional 
coordinator and expressed support for the proposal by the representative of Switzerland. The wording 
“including by involving regional groups” included regional coordinators, who could provide a platform 
for discussion among the leads for Member State-led governance reform and regional representatives, 
while making it clear that there was no expectation of consultations at the regional level, such as within 
regional committees. 
The representative of ETHIOPIA said that she had no objection to the wording, “including by 
involving regional groups”. It would, however, be useful to hold further consultations, including with 
regional committees.  
The CHAIR took it that the Committee wished to approve the proposal by the representative of 
Switzerland to replace, in amended paragraph 2, the words, “assisted by the regional coordinators” with 
the words, “including by involving regional groups”. 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of AUSTRALIA said that, in amended paragraph 2, the words, “Member State 
governance reform” should be amended to read: “Member State-led governance reform”, as in the 
original draft decision.  
It was so agreed. 
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA said that, in amended paragraph 3, 
the insertion of the word “continuing” was intended to reflect that an inclusive process had taken place. 
The representative of AUSTRALIA asked for clarification regarding the meaning of the word 
“open-ended” in amended paragraph 3. 
The LEGAL COUNSEL said that, in amended paragraph 3 and in the context of the Executive 
Board, the word “open-ended” referred to participation by Member States that were not current Board 
members. 
 
1 Participating by virtue of Rule 3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Executive Board.  
 SUMMARY RECORDS: FOURTH MEETING 61 
 
 
 
 
The representative of SLOVAKIA proposed that amended paragraph 3 should be reworded to 
read: “to ensure that the consultations should remain open-ended, maintaining inclusivity and 
transparency.” 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of SLOVAKIA proposed that, in amended paragraph 4, the words, “to consider 
holding regional discussions” should be redrafted to read: “to hold regional discussions”. 
The representative of ETHIOPIA expressed support for the proposal by the representative of 
Slovakia but suggested that in order to ensure that Member States were well informed before decisions 
were made, the words, “to consider holding regional discussions” should be replaced by the words, “to 
hold consultations through the regional committees.” 
The representative of SLOVAKIA asked whether there was a need for all regional committees to 
discuss the draft decision prior to its submission to the Health Assembly since that could delay 
discussions. 
The representative of ETHIOPIA said that the wording should ensure that Member States would 
be well informed on the issue ahead of the Health Assembly, with no intention to reopen discussions on 
the matter. She would welcome broad wording that referred to holding discussions within regional 
committees. 
The representative of AUSTRALIA said that regional engagement was already referred to in 
amended paragraph 2, which set out the related mechanisms, and that the purpose of amended  
paragraph 4 was to urge active participation. He therefore proposed that, in amended paragraph 4, the 
words “and, as appropriate, to consider holding regional discussions among themselves” should be 
deleted. 
The representative of ETHIOPIA said that, in a spirit of flexibility, she proposed that amended 
paragraph 4 should be redrafted to read: “to urge all Member States to participate actively in all 
consultations; and, as appropriate, to hold regional discussions among themselves and consultations 
through the regional committees.”  
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA suggested that amended paragraph 4 
should be reformulated to read: “to urge all Member States to participate actively in all consultations; 
and, as appropriate, to hold regional discussions among themselves, including through the regional 
committees.” 
The representative of AUSTRALIA requested legal clarification of whether the words, “including 
through the regional committees” mandated regional committee participation. He proposed that the last 
part of amended paragraph 4 should instead read: “including through or on the margins of regional 
committees”. 
The LEGAL COUNSEL said that regional committee participation would require a related 
agenda item and therefore the formal preparation of a document to inform discussion. Given that the 
first of the annual regional committee meetings was scheduled to take place in August 2024, timely 
preparation for such a discussion within the regional committees would be challenging. More flexible 
wording could therefore prove helpful. 
The CHAIR took it that the Committee wished to approve amended paragraph 4, which would 
read: “to urge all Member States to participate actively in all consultations; and, as appropriate, to hold 
62 EXECUTIVE BOARD, 155TH SESSION  
 
 
 
 
regional discussions among themselves, including through or on the margins of the regional 
committees;” 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA said that her proposed amendments 
to paragraph 5 reflected the fact that there had been limited time to examine the relevant document and 
therefore called for the leads for Member State-led governance reform to provide briefings on the current 
document as the starting point for discussions. 
The representative of CHILE, expressing support for amended paragraph 5 as proposed by the 
representative of the United States of America, suggested that the word “interested” should be deleted 
from the proposed amended paragraph since briefings should be provided to all WHO regions. 
The representative of SLOVAKIA said that he supported the proposal by the representative of 
Chile. He proposed that amended paragraph 5 should be split into two sentences, with the first sentence 
to finish with the words “revised draft”. The second sentence should then be redrafted to read: “This 
should include initial intersessional briefings on the current document with all WHO regions to foster a 
shared understanding of the approach and to continue incorporating considerations already taken into 
account in developing the procedures presented to the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly.” 
The representative of CHINA proposed that, in the first part of amended paragraph 5, the words, 
“informal progress reports” should be amended to read: “informal briefings.” 
The representative of AUSTRALIA said that, in an effort to remain consistent with the rest of the 
document, in the first part of amended paragraph 5, the word, “co-lead” should be amended to “lead.”  
The CHAIR took it that the Committee wished to approve amended paragraph 5, which would 
read: “to request the leads for Member State-led governance reform, with the support of Secretariat, to 
continue to provide regular informal briefings to Member States regarding development of the revised 
draft. This should include intersessional briefings on the current document with all WHO regions to 
foster a shared understanding of the approach and to continue incorporating considerations already taken 
into account in developing the procedures presented to the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly;” 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of the UNITED STATES OF AMERICA said that the amendments proposed 
to paragraph 6 were aimed at improving the text’s grammar and clarity and ensuring that Member States 
understood who was responsible for the work set out in that paragraph. 
The CHAIR said that, in the absence of any objection, he took it that the Board wished to adopt 
the draft decision as a whole, as amended.  
The decision as a whole, as amended, was adopted.1 
 
1 Decision EB155(12). 
 SUMMARY RECORDS: FOURTH MEETING 63 
 
 
 
 
PILLAR 4: MORE EFFECTIVE AND EFFICIENT WHO PROVIDING BETTER SUPPORT 
TO COUNTRIES (continued) 
2.  FUTURE SESSIONS OF THE EXECUTIVE BOARD AND THE HEALTH ASSEMBLY: 
Item 9 of the agenda (document EB155/12 Rev.1)  
The CHAIR drew the attention of the Board to the report on future sessions of the Executive 
Board and the Health Assembly, contained in document EB155/12 Rev.1. It contained two draft 
decisions relating to the dates of upcoming sessions of the Executive Board, the Programme Budget and 
Administration Committee of the Executive Board, the Standing Committee on Health Emergency 
Prevention, Preparedness and Response, and the Health Assembly. The report also contained proposed 
adjustments to the modalities of those meetings, should any limitations to physical meetings preclude 
the holding of such meetings in person.  
156th session of the Executive Board and forty-first meeting of the Programme, Budget and 
Administration Committee of the Executive Board 
The CHAIR drew attention to the first draft decision contained in document EB155/12 Rev.1. 
The DIRECTOR (Governing Bodies) said that Member States would receive a draft provisional 
agenda for the 156th session of the Executive Board within four weeks of the closure of the current 
session.  
The representative of CHINA said that the proposed dates for the 156th session of the Executive 
Board coincided with the lunar new year festival that was observed by many countries and recognized 
as an official United Nations holiday. She proposed that the session should be convened either one week 
earlier or one week later.  
The representative of THAILAND, echoing the sentiments expressed by the representative of 
China, said that the proposed dates for the 156th session of the Executive Board and forty-first meeting 
of the Programme, Budget and Administration Committee coincided with national festivities. He 
proposed that the 156th session of the Executive Board should be convened on 3 February 2025. 
The representative of the REPUBLIC OF KOREA supported the proposal made by the 
representative of China, owing to traditional new year festivities in her country in January.  
The DIRECTOR (Governing Bodies) said that, convening the Executive Board one week earlier 
would mean that the meeting of the Programme, Budget and Administration Committee would need to 
be convened on 15 January 2025, which would place a burden on the Secretariat and Member States to 
prepare during a time that was a holiday period for many Member States and would increase the risk of 
late documents and incomplete Member State consultations. Although a later start date would lead to 
complications with the election of regional directors, the Legal Counsel had advised that there were 
ways to address these complications. He suggested that the forty-first meeting of the Programme, Budget 
and Administration Committee should be held from 29 January to 31 January 2025, and the  
156th session of the Executive Board from 3 February to 11 February 2025.  
The CHAIR took it that the Board agreed that its 156th session would be held from  
Monday, 3 February 2025, to Tuesday, 11 February 2025, and the Programme, Budget and 
Administration Committee would hold its forty-first meeting from Wednesday, 29 January 2025, to 
Friday, 31 January 2025, at WHO headquarters in Geneva.  
It was so decided.  
64 EXECUTIVE BOARD, 155TH SESSION  
 
 
 
 
Fifth and sixth meetings of the Standing Committee on Health Emergency Prevention, 
Preparedness and Response  
The CHAIR said that he understood that the Board agreed that the fifth meeting of the Standing 
Committee on Health Emergency Prevention, Preparedness and Response would be held on Tuesday 
and Wednesday, 3 and 4 September 2024, and its sixth meeting on Wednesday and Thursday, 16 and 
17 April 2025, at WHO headquarters.  
It was so decided.  
The CHAIR took it that, in the absence of any objections, the Board wished to adopt the first draft 
decision contained in document EB155/12 Rev.1.  
The decision, as amended, was adopted.1 
Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly  
The CHAIR drew attention to the second draft decision contained in document EB155/12 Rev.1. 
He took it that the Board agreed that the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly should be held in 
Geneva, opening on Monday, 19 May 2025, and closing no later than Tuesday, 27 May 2025. 
It was so decided.  
Forty-second meeting of the Programme, Budget and Administration Committee of the 
Executive Board  
The CHAIR said that he understood that the Board agreed that the Programme, Budget and 
Administration Committee of the Executive Board should hold its forty-second meeting from 
Wednesday, 14 to Friday, 16 May 2025, at WHO headquarters in Geneva.  
It was so decided.  
The CHAIR took it that, in the absence of any objections, the Board wished to adopt the second 
draft decision contained in document EB153/12 Rev.1.  
The decision was adopted.2 
The representative of BRAZIL said that it was important for the Organization to take into 
consideration the views expressed during the Health Assembly and Executive Board meetings on the 
need to avoid politicization and polarization and protect participants’ physical and mental health during 
sessions. With more discipline, procedures could be introduced to prevent discussions from leading to 
unnecessary debates or votes. His delegation intended to submit an agenda item on regulating the digital 
marketing of breast-milk substitutes for inclusion on the agenda of the Seventy-eighth World Health 
Assembly. 
The representative of SLOVAKIA, highlighting that there was room for improvement, asked 
whether informal sessions, which had allowed for open, transparent discussions on procedures and 
arrangements in previous years, would be held during the intersessional period. 
 
1 Decision EB155(10). 
2 Decision EB155(11). 
 SUMMARY RECORDS: FOURTH MEETING 65 
 
 
 
 
The representative of CHILE, echoing the question raised by the representative of Slovakia, 
recalled efforts by Member States to introduce mental health as a separate agenda item. She requested 
clarification of the process to include a new item on the agenda of the Health Assembly. A group of 
countries intended to request the inclusion on the agenda of the Seventy-eighth World Health Assembly 
of an item on mental health and would submit a draft decision or draft resolution on the matter at the 
156th session of the Executive Board.  
The representative of CANADA recalled that all Member States had expressed dissatisfaction 
regarding the dense nature of the Health Assembly agenda. The Secretariat and the Executive Board 
should consider how the agenda was planned and which agenda items should be deleted if new items 
were to be added. 
The CHAIR said that Board members would be informed in advance of any informal sessions. 
Right of reply 
The representative of the RUSSIAN FEDERATION, speaking in exercise of the right of reply, 
said that the health situation in Ukraine had been deteriorating for several years, as indicated by statistics 
published by WHO and UNAIDS on socially important diseases. The Government of the Russian 
Federation had started to develop social infrastructure, including health care systems, in territories that 
had decided by referendum to join the Russian Federation. 
3. ELECTION OF CHAIR, VICE-CHAIRS AND RAPPORTEUR: Item 1 of the agenda 
(continued from the first meeting, section 2) 
The CHAIR recalled that Dr Jerome X. Walcott (Barbados) had indicated his availability to Chair 
the Executive Board at its 156th and subsequent sessions. He therefore took it that the Board wished to 
elect Dr Jerome X. Walcott (Barbados) Chair of the Executive Board as of 5 June 2024. 
Mr Walcott (Barbados) was elected Chair. 
The CHAIR-ELECT paid tribute to his predecessors. The current global situation was fraught 
with challenges that significantly impacted global health, yet Member States would be guided by 
multilateralism, consensus-based decision-making, inclusiveness and the shared objective of achieving 
health for all. 
4. CLOSURE OF THE SESSION: Item 10 of the agenda 
The DIRECTOR-GENERAL thanked Member States for their hard work over the session and 
agreed that steps must be taken to protect participants’ health by tackling the organization of the agenda 
and the arrangements for holding meetings of the Executive Board and the Health Assembly. 
After the customary exchange of courtesies, the CHAIR declared the 155th session of the 
Executive Board closed.  
The meeting rose at 16:00.

GENERAL COMMITTEE  
FIRST MEETING 
Monday, 27 May 2024, at 11:55 
Chair: Dr E. DIKOLOTI (Botswana)  
President of the World Health Assembly 
1. ADOPTION OF THE AGENDA AND ALLOCATION OF ITEMS TO THE MAIN 
COMMITTEES: (documents A77/1, A77/1 Add.1 and A77/GC/1) 
The CHAIR reminded the Committee that its terms of reference were set out in Rules 30 to 32 of 
the Rules of Procedure of the World Health Assembly. The provisional agenda was contained in 
document A77/1. The preliminary timetable was contained in document A77/GC/1. 
Proposed supplementary agenda item 
The CHAIR drew attention to a proposal, contained in document A77/1 Add.1, for the inclusion 
of a supplementary agenda item, “Inviting Taiwan to participate in the World Health Assembly as an 
observer”,1 on the provisional agenda of the Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly. The proposal 
had been received from 11 Member States. In line with the procedure followed in previous years, he 
suggested that two delegations should speak in favour of the proposal and two against, following which 
the recommendation not to include the supplementary agenda item would be made. 
It was so agreed. 
The representative of the MARSHALL ISLANDS2 said that the vision established in the WHO 
Constitution of the fundamental right of every human being to the enjoyment of the highest attainable 
standard of health should be upheld by recognizing the population of Taiwan3 and their right to 
participate in the global health security system, including through the participation of Taiwan in the 
Health Assembly as an observer, as had been the case between 2009 and 2016. Global health challenges 
made its participation more important than ever, as part of a more comprehensive global health 
framework to make the world healthier, more resilient and more equitable, and in keeping with the 
establishment in the WHO Constitution of the need for the fullest cooperation in the interests of global 
health. The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic had shown that existing health coverage was 
inadequate; the exclusion of Taiwan impaired disease prevention efforts and jeopardized global health. 
As a responsible global health partner that had alerted WHO early on to cases of COVID-19 and had 
shared vital information on avian influenza, the inclusion of Taiwan would strengthen health emergency 
prevention, preparedness and response. Taiwan had also contributed to global health by improving

of any opinion whatsoever on the part of the Secretariat of the World Health Organization concerning the legal status of any 
country, territory or area, or of its authorities. The terminology used is at variance with that used by the World Health 
Organization. 
2 Participating by virtue of Rule 31 of the Rules of Procedure of the World Health Assembly. 
3 Regarding this and all further such references in the record of the first meeting of the General Committee, World 
Health Organization terminology refers to “Taiwan, China”. 
4 SEVENTY-SEVENTH WORLD HEALTH ASSEMBLY 
 
 
 
 
medical care in small Pacific nations and participating in disaster recovery operations worldwide, 
including by providing support in Haiti and to Ukrainian refugees. He called for a healthier world for 
future generations – a goal that could not be achieved without Taiwan. He urged the Committee to 
support the inclusion and participation of Taiwan in WHO meetings and activities. 
The representative of CHINA expressed his opposition to the inclusion of the proposed 
supplementary item relating to Taiwan on the agenda of the Health Assembly. The proposal lacked a 
legal basis, since the situation of Taiwan was a legacy of the Chinese Civil War and a domestic matter. 
The sovereignty and territory of China had never been divided and the legal status of Taiwan1 as part of 
that territory had not changed. United Nations General Assembly resolution 2758 (XXVI) (1971) and 
resolution WHA25.1 (1972) had resolved the issue of the representation of China, including Taiwan, at 
the United Nations and its specialized agencies, and set out the legal foundation for WHO to follow the 
one-China principle. United Nations documents had defined Taiwan as a province of China, which 
therefore could not participate in the Health Assembly without the consent of the Chinese central 
Government. Taiwan did not belong to any of the current categories of observers to the Health 
Assembly, which were sovereign States, state entities, international organizations and nongovernmental 
organizations. The separatist stance of the Taiwanese authorities had led to the disappearance of political 
space for the participation of Taiwan in the Health Assembly. More than 100 Member States had 
expressed their support for the position of China on the matter. The current proposal did not correspond 
to reality and speculated about the so-called gap in global anti-epidemic efforts; the Chinese central 
Government had approved the participation of Taiwan in WHO technical activities 21 times over the 
previous year, an IHR focal point based in Taiwan ensured prompt communication about health 
emergencies and there were diverse channels for the participation of Taiwan in WHO affairs. He called 
on the Committee to reject the proposal. 
The representative of SAINT LUCIA2 recalled that the WHO Constitution highlighted that the 
health of all peoples was fundamental to the attainment of peace and security and was dependent on the 
fullest cooperation of individuals and States – rendering essential the participation of all stakeholders in 
the Health Assembly, including that of Taiwan as an observer. The prolonged exclusion of Taiwan could 
impair disease prevention efforts and jeopardize global health, while WHO and the international 
community would greatly benefit from its inclusion as a willing and capable partner in a more resilient 
global health architecture and improved health emergency prevention, preparedness and response. 
Taiwan had shown its commitment to universal health coverage and to sharing experience and expertise 
by contributing to global efforts to realize the right to health for all, including by improving medical 
care in the South Pacific, bolstering climate change adaptability in the Caribbean, and supporting 
disaster relief efforts and providing humanitarian assistance in locations across the world. Taiwanese 
officials had reported that incomplete and delayed access to disease-related information had created a 
gap in domestic disease control and global disease prevention. The substantive engagement of Taiwan 
in international mechanisms relating to disease control and in the WHO Regional Office for the Western 
Pacific would enhance the global health system and the fight against communicable diseases. He called 
on the Committee to approve the proposal on the participation of Taiwan in the activities of the Health 
Assembly as an observer. 
The representative of CUBA said that there was only one China and the region of Taiwan was an 
integral and inalienable part of the territory of China. The participation of Taiwan in the work of 
international organizations, including WHO, must be in line with the one-China principle. United 
Nations General Assembly resolution 2758 (XXVI) and resolution WHA25.1 provided a solid legal 
basis for that approach, which was also applied to financial matters, such as the calculation of the 
assessments to the United Nations of the People’s Republic of China. The international community 
broadly supported the fair cause of the Government and people of China. The Government of the 
People’s Republic of China was the only legitimate representative of China, including Taiwan, and its

territorial integrity and sovereignty must be respected without restrictions. Given that the Health 
Assembly had previously made a decision on the matter, he called on the Committee to avoid a 
discussion of the topic at the current session since it would have a negative impact on the discussions 
concerning the important items already on the agenda. 
The CHAIR said that he took it that the Committee wished to recommend that the proposed 
supplementary item should not be included on the provisional agenda of the Seventy-seventh World

It was so agreed.

The CHAIR proposed that a single drafting group, co-chaired by a member of the Bureau of the 
Intergovernmental Negotiating Body and a member of the Bureau of the Working Group on 
Amendments to the International Health Regulations (2005), should be established to consider matters 
related to the ongoing work of the two bodies, starting with the amendments to the Regulations. Such 
an arrangement would promote predictability, transparency and inclusivity and help to avoid parallel 
meetings. 
The representative of SOUTH AFRICA, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the African 
Region, said that, while it was disappointing that consensus had not been reached on the overall text of 
the pandemic agreement, the current outcome should not be considered a failure; it was an important 
step in the process towards a just, fair and legally binding agreement with equity at its core. Although 
progress had been made in the negotiations, much work remained to ensure that the agreement 
effectively delivered the operationalization of equity demanded by Member States in the Region. The 
negotiations must therefore continue under the same Bureau to ensure continuity, and a report should 
be submitted to a special session of the Health Assembly before the end of 2024, on the understanding 
that already agreed text should not be reopened for negotiation. With the necessary political will and 
flexibility, agreement could be reached on key outstanding issues, such as technology transfer and 
know-how, geographically diversified production, pathogen access and benefit-sharing, and sustainable 
financing. The obligations placed on Member States in the areas of prevention, surveillance and the One 
Health approach without the necessary resourcing and capacity could also be agreed. If the pandemic 
agreement were to be meaningful, it must ensure fundamental changes to the status quo, thereby 
strengthening public health systems and capacity and enabling countries to more effectively respond to 
future pandemics. 
The representative of AUSTRALIA, reaffirming his country’s commitment to concluding the 
pandemic agreement, said that his delegation had worked with others from all regions to develop a draft 
resolution setting out the options for Member States going forward, namely to continue the negotiations 
either through the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body or through another body; and to request that the 
outcome of that process be submitted in a report for consideration at a resumed meeting of the 
Seventy-Seventh World Health Assembly, at a special session of the Health Assembly or at a future 
Health Assembly. The text of the cross-regional draft resolution also incorporated the draft resolution 
proposed by the Member States of the African Region. He looked forward to finding consensus on the 
way forward in the drafting group proposed by the Chair so that the path to finalizing the pandemic 
agreement was clear. The time left during the current Health Assembly should be used to finalize and 
adopt the package of amendments to the International Health Regulations (2005). Member States needed

to redouble their efforts to resolve the remaining challenges and achieve better health outcomes for all, 
in responding to future pandemics and public health emergencies.

the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body and in supporting Member States in that process, said that the 
processes to develop an international accord and revise the International Health Regulations (2005) were

prepared for another pandemic. The focus should be on finalizing the amendments to the Regulations

urged to come to the negotiating table with an open mind.

MANUFACTURERS AND ASSOCIATIONS, speaking at the invitation of the CHAIR and also on 
behalf of the Global Self-Care Federation and Global Medical Technology Alliance, said that the life 
sciences industry was committed to developing a pandemic agreement that strengthened countries’ 
ability to respond to the next pandemic, supported the research and development of related vaccines, 
treatments and diagnostics and ensured equitable access to them. A successful pandemic agreement 
would be one that encouraged companies with the right expertise and know-how to develop the science 
and tools needed to respond to a pandemic. Rapid and unconditional access to pathogens and data was

countermeasures should not be based on linking access to pathogen samples and sequence data to

maximum industry participation and delivering equitable access.

timely achievement of a consensus-based pandemic agreement that complemented the strengthened 
International Health Regulations (2005). It was important to draw inspiration from what had been 
achieved thus far in order to continue to make progress on the outstanding issues, which, although

pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, enabling States to work together to reduce inequalities

medical countermeasures, and the rapid and open sharing of samples and data with a clearly defined

The CO-CHAIRS OF THE WORKING GROUP ON AMENDMENTS TO THE 
INTERNATIONAL HEALTH REGULATIONS (2005), speaking in turn to present the results of the 
Working Group, said that, since November 2022, more than 300 proposed amendments to the 
International Health Regulations (2005) submitted by States Parties had been carefully considered, 
discussed and refined. The recommendations of the Review Committee regarding amendments to the 
International Health Regulations (2005) had provided a solid basis for the work of the Working Group; 
the Committee’s final report and the interest and contributions from civil society organization had also 
proved invaluable. Applauding participants’ extraordinary commitment and outstanding spirit of 
negotiation during the Working Group’s numerous meetings, they expressed appreciation for the trust 
placed in the Bureau of the Working Group and for the Secretariat’s excellent advice and active support. 
Every effort had been made to develop a package of targeted amendments designed to strengthen 
and update the Regulations. Importantly, throughout the process, there had been an unwavering and 
universal commitment to incorporating equity-related provisions. The Working Group was very close 
to producing an agreed package of amendments. Some of the historic amendments proposed had already 
been agreed, and there was momentum and an aspiration among participants to complete the task.  
Finalizing and adopting a package of amendments that would make the Regulations fairer, more 
exhaustive and equitable would be a significant achievement, and would constitute a stepping stone 
towards the successful conclusion of the negotiations on a pandemic agreement. The Working Group 
stood ready to continue discussions in the coming days, so that the amendments could be adopted by the 
Seventy-seventh World Health Assembly.

Mediterranean Region, said that the Region, which continued to face escalating emergencies, recognized 
the importance of the International Health Regulations (2005) in preventing and responding to health 
threats and mitigating the spread of diseases. The decision by Member States, following the COVID-19 
pandemic, to explore potential targeted amendments to the Regulations to enhance their effectiveness, 
promote compliance and address gaps demonstrated their collective commitment to strengthening global 
health security. Noting that equity, solidarity, international cooperation, trust-building, transparency and 
sovereignty had been cross-cutting themes in the amendment process, he said that the proposed 
amendments should enhance Member States’ capacities relating to health emergency and pandemic

accessible, available and affordable for everyone and everywhere, to accelerate progress to

anesthesia, and nursing services for injuries, structural birth defects, which will proportionally 
increase as child survival improves,4 and other acute emergencies, will result in unacceptable

(PP9) Noting the importance of infection prevention and control programmes in health care 
facilities, and noting with concern the increasing burden of health care-associated infections, often 
by antibiotic-resistant pathogens, which harm patients and health care providers and usually

lack basic hand hygiene services;

multisectoral national action plans on antimicrobial resistance, but Tracking Antimicrobial

capacities and availability of technical and funding support;

priorities to address drug-resistant bacterial infections in the human health sector, 2025–2035,

research and development for vaccines, diagnostics and treatments; and (d) effective governance 
and financing of the human health sector response to antimicrobial resistance – all of which will 
support a broad, health system-wide response to antimicrobial resistance;

The representative of BELGIUM, speaking on behalf of the European Union and its Member 
States, said that the Member States of the European Union wished to be added to the list of sponsors of 
the draft resolution on accelerating progress towards reducing maternal, newborn and child mortality in 
order to achieve Sustainable Development Goal targets 3.1 and 3.2.  
Welcoming the inclusion of antimicrobial resistance on the agenda, she said that the candidate 
countries Türkiye, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, 
Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia, the EFTA countries Iceland and Norway, members of the 
European Economic Area, as well as Armenia, aligned themselves with her statement. Antimicrobial 
resistance was driven by a lack of regulation and guidance on the use of antimicrobial agents, and climate 
change and humanitarian crises, and was exacerbated by inequality. Responsible use of antimicrobial 
agents and high standards of surveillance, prevention and control were key. Evidence-based WHO 
guidance was welcome, since tackling antimicrobial resistance required the availability of, and access 
to, safe and effective antimicrobial agents, vaccines and diagnostics. She encouraged support for 
research and development and access to new and existing antimicrobial agents and other medical 
technologies, through collaboration with academic institutions, civil society organizations and the 
private sector. The Secretariat should develop more evidence-based and cost-effective policy measures 
to ensure prudent use of antimicrobial agents; existing measures were too focused on passive strategies 
that were insufficient to achieve the necessary targets. More emphasis was needed on structural and 
prescriptive measures. Negotiations on a high-level political declaration on antimicrobial resistance 
must be accompanied by strong political commitment; she called for the setting of tangible objectives 
and measurable targets, as well as measures to integrate the One Health approach at all levels.  
A whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach was essential, as were efforts to ensure 
sufficient and sustainable funding. She called on the Secretariat to continue its strong collaboration with 
other quadripartite organizations.

The representative of YEMEN, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the Eastern 
Mediterranean Region and referring to items 13.1 and 13.2, said that the Secretariat’s technical team

Regulations (2005) as the main international tool to combat the spread of disease. Unfortunately, their

(COVID-19) pandemic had failed to translate into improved scores in the States Parties Self-assessment 
annual reporting tool and in some areas, notably with regard to entry points, had regressed to previous

difficult to sustain the gains made during the pandemic. In order not to miss opportunities for progress, 
it was important to strengthen capacities and break the cycle of pandemic, alarm and neglect. It was also 
necessary to reflect on some of the broader lessons learned from COVID-19 and other recent pandemics.

investment in emergency preparedness. The Member States of the Region strongly recommended:

The representative of the BAHAMAS said that her country had, with the Secretariat’s technical 
support, implemented integrated, people-centred eye care for conditions such as diabetic retinopathy

Treatment and Care, underscoring the need for a strong multisectoral response in that regard. 
The representative of GHANA said that while progress had been made on HIV prevention, 
diagnosis and treatment, gaps persisted in her country. She urged the Secretariat to continue to provide 
support for the smooth and sustainable implementation of routine human papillomavirus vaccination. 
The international community must increase investment in health systems and strengthen research and 
development and capacity-building to accelerate progress. 
The representative of BRAZIL said that the global health sector strategies on, respectively, HIV, 
viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, for the period 2022–2030, were aligned with her

on public health, innovation and intellectual property. It was essential to increase transparency in

The representative of SENEGAL said that the global health sector strategies on, respectively, 
HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, for the period 2022–2030, enabled countries to

The representative of CHILE welcomed the global health sector strategies on, respectively, HIV,

Her Government stood ready to work with a range of social actors, government bodies and cooperation 
agencies to achieve the related objectives and targets.  
The representative of FIJI, acknowledging the progress report on the global health sector 
strategies on, respectively, HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, for the period

whole-of-government and whole-of-society response.

The representative of MEXICO said that the Organization’s efforts to strengthen its integration 
of gender analysis must be sustainable and sufficiently resourced over the long term. Similarly, an

The representative of the ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN requested technical and logistics

The representative of the RUSSIAN FEDERATION expressed support for the global health 
sector strategies on, respectively, HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, for the period

The representative of CHINA said that implementation of the global health sector strategies on, 
respectively, HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections, for the period 2022–2030, should

methodologies and monitoring capacities should be strengthened to accelerate the eradication of

The representative of SPAIN said that, given the clear upward trend in the number of cases of 
sexually transmitted infections, their detrimental effects on human health, rising resistance to treatment

transmitted infections, beyond World AIDS Day and World Sexual Health Day, in order to enhance 
their visibility and improve control. 
The representative of NAMIBIA said that her Government’s achievements towards ending AIDS 
as a public health threat by 2030 and eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV and hepatitis B 
were threatened by several challenges, including reduced external funding. The Secretariat should 
therefore consider engaging with global financial entities to promote debt relief as a mechanism to 
ensure financial sustainability. It should also support country-specific interventions to improve 
sustainability. 
The representative of IRAQ welcomed the Secretariat’s support in developing a strategy to 
address HIV, hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections in her country, and shared information on 
initiatives relating to eye care and influenza monitoring, surveillance and vaccination. 
The representative of INDONESIA called for support in strengthening evidence-based  
policy-making to ensure that communities had access to cost-effective technologies and sustainable 
health financing; enhancing capacities through health workforce training and infrastructure 
development; raising public health awareness and promoting disease prevention; implementing health

The representative of COLOMBIA, speaking on behalf of Andorra, Armenia, Australia, Belgium, 
the Plurinational State of Bolivia, Brazil, Canada, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, 
Denmark, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Estonia, Finland, Georgia, Greece, Guatemala, Hungary, 
Ireland, Jamaica, Kiribati, Latvia, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, New Zealand, 
Norway, Panama, Portugal, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Switzerland, 
Ukraine and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, recognized the crucial role 
played by WHO in promoting efforts to address the health dimension of the world drug problem; the 
need for drug control measures that covered the entire public health continuum and were grounded in 
the fundamental public health principles of equity, individual freedom, social justice and human rights; 
and the importance of increasing efforts to mobilize resources and strengthen WHO’s capacity to address 
those issues. 
He welcomed the actions outlined in the report, including the development of WHO guidance on 
mental health and drug consumption, on access to controlled medicines and on the management of 
opioids overdose, and its work with other agencies of the United Nations system, particularly UNODC 
and INCB. However, urgent action was needed to address the persistent, unprecedented and expanding 
challenges related to drug use, including the impact on health systems, rapidly evolving illicit drug 
manufacturing and trafficking, and the proliferation of illicit synthetic drugs. Millions of people, 
especially in developing countries, continued to suffer as a result of inadequate access to, and availability 
of, affordable controlled medicines. Such drug-related issues had a direct impact on people’s right to 
health and well-being. Drug use disorders were multifactorial health conditions that could be addressed 
only through inclusive, rights-based, non-discriminatory and stigma-free care, harm reduction, social 
protection and rehabilitation. Governments should ally more strongly with civil society and the private 
sector to that end. 
The international drug control system must be rethought, using an evidence-based approach with 
common goals and objectives, including by fostering greater coherence and exchanges throughout the 
United Nations system and better engagement with civil society. The public health dimension of drugs 
policies must once again become a priority of WHO’s work, and Member States should engage 
constructively to prioritize public health, develop prevention initiatives and destigmatize drug use and 
related disorders, while ensuring access to, and the availability of, controlled substances for medical and 
scientific purposes, including pain relief. Global solidarity and cooperation must reduce the immense 
human suffering caused by the worldwide phenomenon, through a transformed, evidence-based and 
pragmatic approach.

The representative of the INTERNATIONAL AIDS SOCIETY, speaking at the invitation of the

treatments for that disease existed, they were often difficult to administer and access to them was limited. 
In addition, Member States must urgently remove barriers to hepatitis C diagnosis and treatment, 
including patent barriers, and include new, affordable, direct-acting antiviral medicines in national 
essential medicines lists.  
The representative of the INTERNATIONAL PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION,

The ASSISTANT DIRECTOR-GENERAL (Access to Medicines and Health Products) 
(Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim) thanked Member States for highlighting the importance of access 
to quality-assured, safe, effective and affordable health products in order to achieve universal health 
coverage and other Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the need for access to controlled 
medicines, such as narcotic drugs for pain control, which was complicated by the need to avoid their 
harmful use. The Secretariat had been working closely with UNODC to ensure access to medicines 
subject to international drug control treaties, and had published a report in 2023 on the disparity in 
morphine access and ways to improve access and affordability. Comprehensive recommendations would 
be issued later in the year 2024 on policy initiatives that countries could take to ensure balanced, 
equitable and safe access to controlled medicines. The Secretariat would also update the road map for 
access to medicines, vaccines and other health products 2019–2023, and hold consultations with 
Member States in that regard in 2024.

The CHAIR OF THE PROGRAMME, BUDGET AND ADMINISTRATION COMMITTEE OF 
THE EXECUTIVE BOARD presented the reports of the Programme, Budget and Administration 
Committee on budget and finance matters. The Committee had recommended that the Health Assembly 
note the reports contained in documents A77/19 and A77/20, and adopt the draft decision on the Results 
Report 2023 (Programme budget 2022–2023: performance assessment) and the audited financial 
statements for the year ended 31 December 2023, contained in document A77/36, and the draft

The HEAD OF ACCOUNTS AND FINANCIAL REPORTING said that, since the Programme, 
Budget and Administration Committee had met, Lesotho had paid its arrears and was no longer subject 
to Article 7. 
The representative of CABO VERDE, speaking on behalf of the Member States of the African 
Region, said that the Secretariat’s technical and financial support and the transparent allocation of 
resources had significantly boosted health outcomes in Africa. Continued commitment during the final 
biennium of the Thirteenth General Programme of Work, 2019–2025, was essential to achieve the triple 
billion targets. Improved maternal and child health services, expanded vaccination programmes and 
Cabo Verde’s recent malaria-free certification were evidence of the tangible benefits of African Member 
States’ commitment to bolstering health systems and attaining the Sustainable Development Goals. 
WHO needed more support to create a healthier world and help the countries of the Region to achieve 
the results anticipated in the Organization’s general programmes of work. In line with Article 7 of the 
Constitution, all Member States must pay their assessed contributions in full and on time, and take 
appropriate steps to pay any arrears. 
The representative of MEXICO expressed concern that, despite significant progress in several 
areas, universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals were far from being achieved. 
The Secretariat should analyse country-specific challenges and provide support and guidance to 
implement national policies and plans, and to bridge gaps. Noting that US$ 79 million had been released 
from the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies within 24 hours to respond to 22 graded emergencies 
in 2023, she requested further information about the specific items for which those resources had been 
used. Resource availability should not be the sole focus in achieving the sustainable financing of WHO; 
it was also essential to ensure adequate results-oriented implementation, financial flexibility, 
transparency and accountability, achieve savings and continue to set appropriate priorities by 
considering WHO’s added value. Member States and the Secretariat should commit to optimizing the 
use of resources, based on priorities and availability. 
The representative of ARGENTINA welcomed the widespread use by country offices of the 
enhanced and simplified output scorecard. While strides had been made towards achieving universal 
health coverage and healthier populations, her Government agreed on the need to redouble efforts and 
focus all resources on an attainable subset of the triple billion targets and the health-related Sustainable 
Development Goals. All countries in the Region of the Americas should move forward with smart 
spending models. 
The representative of INDIA said that she welcomed the streamlined output scorecard and its 
emphasis on self-reflection for organizational learning and accountability. Describing national efforts 
to improve health, she acknowledged the global challenges to achieving the triple billion targets and the 
Sustainable Development Goals, and expressed support for the Secretariat’s initiatives on data 
availability, digital health and gender equality, and its aim to strengthen country office capacities while 
balancing investments in normative functions. The Results Report 2023 could be made more useful by

international humanitarian law and end the war. Overcrowded camps for internally displaced persons

The representative of SAUDI ARABIA expressed appreciation for the Secretariat’s efforts 
concerning the implementation of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and 
the guidance on ending the inappropriate promotion of foods for infants and young children. It was 
important to implement measures restricting the digital marketing of breast-milk substitutes and increase 
public awareness of the issue. His Government was committed to implementing the global framework 
for integrating well-being into public health utilizing a health promotion approach and to addressing the 
social determinants of health. Given the close interrelationship between economic development and 
health, he highlighted the importance of a whole-of-government approach and increased investment, 
sustainable financing and innovation for health. 
The representative of BRAZIL, speaking also on behalf of Armenia, Bangladesh, Belgium, the 
Plurinational State of Bolivia, Botswana, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador,
